# The Bias Atlas series

> The Bias Atlas series from Conyso Publishing: books built from the Bias Atlas, Conyso's free, sourced map of cognitive biases. No titles announced yet.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/bias-atlas-series.html

A Conyso Publishing series

# The Bias Atlas series

The Bias Atlas series will turn [the Bias Atlas](https://conyso.com/biases/), Conyso's free map of cognitive biases, into books: thinking errors, how to spot them and which findings held up. Like the Law Tome series, every book is built from sourced records and checked against them.

## Which books are in it?

No titles announced yet. They will be listed here when they are ready.

The other series is [the Law Tome series](https://conyso.com/publishing/law-tome-series.html). Its first book, [*True or Folklore?*](https://conyso.com/publishing/true-or-folklore.html), is coming soon.

# Did 38 witnesses watch Kitty Genovese die and do nothing?

> Did 38 witnesses watch Kitty Genovese die and do nothing? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-38-witnesses-watch-kitty-genovese-die-and-do-nothing.html

Story No. 21 · [Round 3: Famous experiments, retold](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-03.html)

# Did 38 witnesses watch Kitty Genovese die and do nothing?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The record finds no basis for the story that 38 witnesses watched Kitty Genovese die and did nothing. At least one witness shouted at her attacker.

Tell someone: The record finds no basis for 38 silent witnesses to Kitty Genovese's murder, and at least one witness shouted at her attacker.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is short and bleak. Kitty Genovese was murdered in 1964 while 38 people watched, and not one of them acted. It is often told as proof that a crowd will leave a person to die.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Manning, Levine & Collins 2007 abstract via Europe PMC](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=DOI:10.1037/0003-066X.62.6.555)
- [Philpot et al. 2020 abstract via Europe PMC](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=DOI:10.1037/amp0000469)
- ["Murder of Kitty Genovese," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_Kitty_Genovese)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Manning, Levine & Collins, "The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping," *American Psychologist* 62(6) (2007). Philpot et al., "Would I be helped? Cross-national CCTV footage shows that intervention is the norm in public conflicts," *American Psychologist* (2020). "Bystander effect," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/the-bystander-effect/).

# Did 65% of Milgram's volunteers give the maximum shock?

> Did 65% of Milgram's volunteers give the maximum shock? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-65-of-milgrams-volunteers-give-the-maximum-shock.html

Story No. 24 · [Round 3: Famous experiments, retold](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-03.html)

# Did 65% of Milgram's volunteers give the maximum shock?

Just show me the answer

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** About 65 percent of participants went to the maximum 450 volts in one baseline condition. Across the more than twenty conditions Milgram ran, obedience varied widely, and archival research has questioned how many participants believed the shocks were real.

Tell someone: Milgram's famous 65 percent came from one baseline condition, obedience varied widely across his variants, and how many believed the shocks were real is disputed.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version turns that number into a fact about people. Two-thirds of ordinary people, it says, will deliver a seemingly lethal shock to a stranger if someone in authority tells them to.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- ["Milgram experiment," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milgram_experiment)
- [Haslam, Loughnan & Perry 2014 abstract via Europe PMC](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=DOI:10.1371/journal.pone.0093927)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Milgram, "Behavioral Study of Obedience," *Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology* (1963). Perry, *Behind the Shock Machine* (2012). Haslam, Loughnan & Perry, "Meta-Milgram," *PLOS ONE* (2014). "Milgram experiment," Wikipedia. "Milgram experiment," *Encyclopaedia Britannica*. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/the-milgram-experiment/).

# Did a cobra bounty in Delhi breed more cobras?

> Did a cobra bounty in Delhi breed more cobras? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-a-cobra-bounty-in-delhi-breed-more-cobras.html

Story No. 91 · [Round 10: Money, power and policy](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-10.html)

# Did a cobra bounty in Delhi breed more cobras?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** No record shows that anyone in Delhi bred cobras for a bounty. The idea the story named rests on firmer evidence, which is the next story in this round.

Tell someone: The cobra-breeding story, usually set in Delhi, traces to an 1873 report on a Madras bounty saying only that it "was alleged," yet an economist named an effect after it.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is short. British officials in colonial Delhi paid a reward for dead cobras, and local people started breeding cobras to collect it. The German economist Horst Siebert liked the story enough to name an idea after it. His 2001 book *Der Kobra-Effekt* describes how a reward offered to solve a problem can end up paying people to manufacture it.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Friends of Snakes Society, "Cobra effect"](https://friendsofsnakes.org.in/cobra-effect/)
- [Davis (2008), EconPapers abstract](https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:ucp:jpolec:v:116:y:2008:i:1:p:38-81)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Siebert, *Der Kobra-Effekt* (2001). Friends of Snakes Society review (2025), citing the *Morning Advertiser*, 23 September 1873. Davis, *Journal of Political Economy* 116 (2008). The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/cobra-effect/).

# Did a French bounty on rat tails in Hanoi backfire?

> Did a French bounty on rat tails in Hanoi backfire? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-a-french-bounty-on-rat-tails-in-hanoi-backfire.html

Story No. 92 · [Round 10: Money, power and policy](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-10.html)

# Did a French bounty on rat tails in Hanoi backfire?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** In 1902 the French colonial administration in Hanoi paid a bounty for each rat killed, with a severed tail as proof. Rat-catchers began cutting the tails off live rats and letting them go to breed. The case is documented in a 2003 paper by M. G. Vann in *French Colonial History*.

Tell someone: Hanoi's 1902 rat bounty took tails as proof, so rat-catchers cut the tails off live rats and released them to breed.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is the same story, which is the surprise. Paying for tails produced rats without tails, and rats without tails went on producing rats. It sounds too neat to be true, and it shares a shape with the Delhi cobra story, which the record treats as folklore.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Vann interview, Made in China Journal](https://madeinchinajournal.com/2020/08/20/the-great-hanoi-rat-hunt)
- [CFPB release](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/about-us/newsroom/consumer-financial-protection-bureau-fines-wells-fargo-100-million-widespread-illegal-practice-secretly-opening-unauthorized-accounts/)
- [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/2020/10/01/digitalocean_hacktoberfest_pull_request_spam/)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Vann, "Of Rats, Rice, and Race," *French Colonial History* 4 (2003). Siebert, *Der Kobra-Effekt* (2001). "Perverse incentive," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/cobra-effect/).

# Did a real Robert Hanlon coin Hanlon's razor?

> Did a real Robert Hanlon coin Hanlon's razor? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-a-real-robert-hanlon-coin-hanlons-razor.html

Story No. 15 · [Round 2: Who really said it?](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-02.html)

# Did a real Robert Hanlon coin Hanlon's razor?

Just show me the answer

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** The razor is generally credited to a Robert J. Hanlon, but the evidence for him is second-hand. Its first appearance in print, in a 1980 book, gives the name "Hanlon" with no indication of who he was.

Tell someone: Hanlon's razor first appeared in print in a 1980 book, but the evidence that a real Robert J. Hanlon wrote it is second-hand.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is that a man named Hanlon coined the line "Never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity," and that the razor bears his name for that reason.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Quote Investigator](https://quoteinvestigator.com/2016/12/30/not-malice/)
- ["Hanlon's razor," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanlon%27s_razor)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Bloch, *Murphy's Law Book Two* (1980), p. 52. Heinlein, "Logic of Empire," *Astounding Science Fiction* (March 1941). Quote Investigator (2016). The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/hanlons-razor/).

# Did Abraham Wald draw the famous bullet-hole plane?

> Did Abraham Wald draw the famous bullet-hole plane? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-abraham-wald-draw-the-famous-bullet-hole-plane.html

Story No. 35 · [Round 4: Charts and numbers](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-04.html)

# Did Abraham Wald draw the famous bullet-hole plane?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Abraham Wald did not draw the bomber covered in red dots. The record describes that image as a designer's later recreation, a teaching device from decades after the war.

Tell someone: Abraham Wald's 1943 memoranda were dense probability, not a sketch, and the red-dotted bomber is a designer's later recreation, drawn decades after the war.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version comes with a picture. A plane seen from above is spattered with red dots where returning bombers were hit. Wald, studying it, tells the military to armor the clean areas instead.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Cameron Moll](https://cameronmoll.com/journal/abraham-wald-red-bullet-holes-origin-story)
- [Yuxi Liu, "That Survivorship Bias Plane"](https://yuxi.ml/logs/posts/2025-survivorship-bias)
- ["Survivorship bias," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survivorship_bias)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Wald, "A Method of Estimating Plane Vulnerability Based on Damage of Survivors" (1943; Center for Naval Analyses reprint, 1980). Moll, "Abraham Wald and the airplane diagram with red bullet holes – here's the origin story," cameronmoll.com (24 March 2022). "Survivorship bias," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/survivorship-bias/).

# Did an apple fall on Newton's head?

> Did an apple fall on Newton's head? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-an-apple-fall-on-newtons-head.html

Story No. 2 · [Round 1: Famous scenes](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-01.html)

# Did an apple fall on Newton's head?

![Cartoon for the question: Did an apple fall on Newton's head?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/002.png)

FOLKLORE

Just show me the answer

**Folklore.** There is an apple in Newton's own account of his thinking about gravity. It does not hit him on the head. That detail is a later embellishment.

Tell someone: According to *Britannica*, Newton's own recollection includes an apple but no bump; the hit on the head was a later embellishment.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is a piece of slapstick. An apple dropped onto Newton's head, and the idea of gravity arrived with the bump.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Stukeley transcription, physics.info](https://physics.info/gravitation/quote-newton.shtml)
- [Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/blog/observations/whats-the-real-story-with-newton-and-the-apple-see-for-yourself/)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Stukeley, *Memoirs of Sir Isaac Newton's Life* (1752). "Newton's law of gravitation," *Encyclopaedia Britannica*. "Newton's law of universal gravitation," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/newtons-law-of-universal-gravitation/).

# Did Archimedes shout "Eureka!" in the bath?

> Did Archimedes shout "Eureka!" in the bath? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-archimedes-shout-eureka-in-the-bath.html

Story No. 1 · [Round 1: Famous scenes](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-01.html)

# Did Archimedes shout "Eureka!" in the bath?

![Cartoon for the question: Did Archimedes shout "Eureka!" in the bath?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/001.png)

FOLKLORE

Just show me the answer

**Folklore.** Archimedes stated the law of buoyancy around 250 BC, in his treatise *On Floating Bodies*. The bath, the crown and the cry of "Eureka!" are almost certainly a later embellishment.

Tell someone: Archimedes did state the law of buoyancy, but the bath and the "Eureka!" almost certainly come from Vitruvius, writing some two centuries later.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is a single moment. Archimedes stepped into his bath, saw the water rise, and realized how to settle a problem about a crown. He ran out shouting "Eureka!"

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Vitruvius, Gwilt translation, LacusCurtius](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Vitruvius/9*.html)
- [Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/fact-or-fiction-archimede/)
- [Rorres, NYU](https://www.math.nyu.edu/~crorres/Archimedes/Crown/CrownIntro.html)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Vitruvius, *De architectura*, book IX, preface. "Fact or Fiction?: Archimedes Coined the Term 'Eureka!' in the Bath," *Scientific American*. Rorres, "The Golden Crown," NYU. "Archimedes' principle," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/archimedes-principle/).

# Did broken-windows policing cause New York's 1990s crime drop?

> Did broken-windows policing cause New York's 1990s crime drop? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-broken-windows-policing-cause-new-yorks-1990s-crime-drop.html

Story No. 95 · [Round 10: Money, power and policy](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-10.html)

# Did broken-windows policing cause New York's 1990s crime drop?

Just show me the answer

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** The claim that broken-windows policing caused New York's crime decline is disputed and confounded. Crime fell across most American cities in the 1990s, including cities that never adopted the approach, and a 2006 analysis by Harcourt and Ludwig found little causal support for the crime-reduction claim.

Tell someone: Crime fell across most American cities in the 1990s, including ones that never tried broken-windows policing, so its credit for New York's drop remains disputed.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version credits the windows. New York fixed the small things, arrested fare-dodgers and cleaned off graffiti, and the city became safe.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Wilson and Kelling, "Broken Windows," Manhattan Institute PDF of the Atlantic text](https://manhattan.institute/pdf/_atlantic_monthly-broken_windows.pdf)
- [Harcourt and Ludwig abstract](https://scholarship.law.columbia.edu/faculty_scholarship/1371)
- [Keizer et al., University of Groningen copy](https://pure.rug.nl/ws/files/10429297/KeizerK-Spreading-2008.pdf)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Wilson and Kelling, "Broken Windows," *The Atlantic Monthly* (1982). Keizer, Lindenberg and Steg, *Science* 322 (2008). Harcourt and Ludwig, *University of Chicago Law Review* 73(1) (2006). The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/the-broken-windows-theory/).

# Did Brooks admit his own law was an oversimplification?

> Did Brooks admit his own law was an oversimplification? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-brooks-admit-his-own-law-was-an-oversimplification.html

Story No. 74 · [Round 8: Jokes that became laws](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-08.html)

# Did Brooks admit his own law was an oversimplification?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** Fred Brooks, who coined Brooks's law in *The Mythical Man-Month* (1975), freely admitted that the law oversimplifies a real tendency: he introduced it with the words "Oversimplifying outrageously."

Tell someone: Fred Brooks introduced his own law, that adding manpower to a late software project makes it later, with the words "Oversimplifying outrageously."

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version treats it as an iron law of software: never add people to a late project, because it will only get later.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Fred Brooks, Wikiquote](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Fred_Brooks)
- [akos.ma, "Adding manpower," quoting the 1995 ed.](https://akos.ma/blog/adding-manpower/)
- ["Brooks's law," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooks%27s_law)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Brooks, *The Mythical Man-Month* (1975; anniversary ed. 1995). "Brooks's law," Wikipedia. "The Mythical Man-Month," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/brooks-law/).

# Did Churchill promise "blood, sweat and tears"?

> Did Churchill promise "blood, sweat and tears"? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-churchill-promise-blood-sweat-and-tears.html

Story No. 9 · [Round 1: Famous scenes](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-01.html)

# Did Churchill promise "blood, sweat and tears"?

![Cartoon for the question: Did Churchill promise "blood, sweat and tears"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/009.png)

FOLKLORE

Just show me the answer

**Folklore.** In May 1940 Churchill offered "blood, toil, tears and sweat." That is four items, not three, and "toil" is the word that dropped out.

Tell someone: Churchill offered "blood, toil, tears and sweat" in May 1940: four items, and "toil" is the word that dropped out.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is the three-word phrase almost everyone quotes: Churchill, in May 1940, offering the nation blood, sweat and tears.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Hansard, HC Deb 13 May 1940](https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1940/may/13/his-majestys-government-1)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Hansard, HC Deb 13 May 1940. "Rule of three (writing)," Wikipedia. "Tricolon," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/the-rule-of-three/).

# Did Clarke add "Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic" years later?

> Did Clarke add "Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic" years later? Guess first, then see the verdict and its source.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-clarke-add-any-sufficiently-advanced-technology-is-indistinguishable-from-magic-years-later.html

Story No. 75 · [Round 8: Jokes that became laws](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-08.html)

# Did Clarke add "Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic" years later?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** Arthur C. Clarke's most famous law came last. He stated his First and Second Laws in 1962 and added the Third, "Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic," to the revised 1973 edition of the same book, having first published it in a 1968 letter to *Science*.

Tell someone: Clarke's First and Second Laws date from 1962; the magic one came last, in a 1968 letter to *Science*, joining the book in 1973.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version treats the three laws as a set, written together.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- ["Clarke's three laws," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarke%27s_three_laws)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Clarke, "Hazards of Prophecy: The Failure of Imagination," in *Profiles of the Future* (1962; rev. 1973). "Clarke's three laws," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/clarkes-three-laws/).

# Did Clausewitz coin "the fog of war"?

> Did Clausewitz coin "the fog of war"? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-clausewitz-coin-the-fog-of-war.html

Story No. 66 · [Round 7: Words and phrases](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-07.html)

# Did Clausewitz coin "the fog of war"?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Carl von Clausewitz did not coin "the fog of war." In *On War* (1832) he conveyed the uncertainty of war through images of fog, twilight and moonlight. The crisp phrase is a later paraphrase, prominent partly because a twentieth-century translation chose the word "fog."

Tell someone: Clausewitz wrote of fog, twilight and moonlight in *On War*, but the tidy phrase "the fog of war" came later from translators and interpreters.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version presents "the fog of war" as a phrase lifted straight from *On War*, the Prussian theorist's own coinage.

## What's the source?

Cited in the book: Clausewitz, *On War*, Book 1, Chapter 3 and Book 2, Chapter 2 (Graham translation, 1873). "Fog of war," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/the-fog-of-war/).

# Did Edward Murphy say "Anything that can go wrong will go wrong"?

![Cartoon for the question: Did Edward Murphy say "Anything that can go wrong will go wrong"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/010.png)

DISPUTED

Just show me the answer

**Disputed.** A maxim like it came out of an Air Force rocket-sled project around 1949, and Murphy's name stuck to it. Who first said it, and in what words, is not settled. The earliest firm printing under Murphy's name, from 1952, credits an unnamed physicist.

Tell someone: Who first said Murphy's law is disputed; its earliest firm printing under his name, in 1952, credits an unnamed physicist.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version has an engineer called Murphy, annoyed by a botched job, coining the law on the spot.

## What's the source?

- ["Murphy's law," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murphy%27s_law)

# Did Einstein win his Nobel Prize for something other than relativity?

> Did Einstein win his Nobel Prize for something other than relativity? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-einstein-win-his-nobel-prize-for-something-other-than-relativity.html

Story No. 7 · [Round 1: Famous scenes](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-01.html)

# Did Einstein win his Nobel Prize for something other than relativity?

![Cartoon for the question: Did Einstein win his Nobel Prize for something other than relativity?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/007.png)

TRUE

Just show me the answer

**True.** Einstein's Nobel Prize, the physics prize designated for 1921, was for his work on the photoelectric effect. NobelPrize.org gives the citation as "for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect." Relativity is not what the prize named.

Tell someone: Einstein's Nobel was not for relativity: the prize designated for 1921 named his law of the photoelectric effect.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version assumes the obvious. Einstein is famous for relativity, so the Nobel committee must have given him the prize for relativity.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [NobelPrize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1921/summary/)
- [APS Physics 18, 12](https://physics.aps.org/articles/v18/12)
- [APS Historic Sites](https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/history/historicsites/millikan.cfm)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Einstein, *Annalen der Physik* 322(6) (1905). The Nobel Prize in Physics 1921, NobelPrize.org. "Millikan's Measurement of Planck's Constant," APS Physics. "Robert Millikan," APS Historic Sites. "Photoelectric effect," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/the-photoelectric-effect/).

FOLKLORE

The popular version has Einstein setting down E = mc² in one short line in 1905, the equation appearing fully formed in the paper that announced it.

# Did Fermi pose the Fermi paradox over lunch?

> Did Fermi pose the Fermi paradox over lunch? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-fermi-pose-the-fermi-paradox-over-lunch.html

Story No. 80 · [Round 8: Jokes that became laws](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-08.html)

# Did Fermi pose the Fermi paradox over lunch?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** The question began as a lunchtime remark by the physicist Enrico Fermi at Los Alamos in 1950, with his colleagues Teller, Konopinski and York. Firsthand accounts differ on his exact words, and the paradox's name and rigorous form came later, from others.

Tell someone: Fermi did raise the question over lunch at Los Alamos in 1950, though firsthand accounts differ on his exact words.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version has Fermi at lunch asking, "Where is everybody?" and launching the paradox on the spot.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Jones, LA-10311-MS, OSTI](https://www.osti.gov/biblio/5746675)
- ["Fermi paradox," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermi_paradox)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Jones, "Where is everybody?" An account of Fermi's question, Los Alamos LA-10311-MS (1985). "Fermi paradox," Wikipedia. "Fermi paradox," *Encyclopaedia Britannica*. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/fermi-paradox/).

# Did Galileo drop balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa?

![Cartoon for the question: Did Galileo drop balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/004.png)

FOLKLORE

Just show me the answer

**Folklore.** The tower drop is likely a legend. It is not in Galileo's own writings. His documented work on falling bodies used balls rolling down ramps, with notes from around 1603 to 1604 and results published in 1638.

Tell someone: The tower drop is likely a legend; Galileo's documented work on falling bodies rolled balls down ramps and timed them with a water clock.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is a public demonstration. Galileo climbed the Leaning Tower of Pisa, let go of a heavy weight and a light one together, and proved that both fall at the same rate.

## What's the source?

- ["Galileo's Leaning Tower of Pisa experiment," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo%27s_Leaning_Tower_of_Pisa_experiment)

# Did Gauss guess the prime number theorem as a teenager?

# Did Godwin say whoever mentions Hitler first loses?

> Did Godwin say whoever mentions Hitler first loses? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-godwin-say-whoever-mentions-hitler-first-loses.html

Story No. 17 · [Round 2: Who really said it?](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-02.html)

# Did Godwin say whoever mentions Hitler first loses?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Mike Godwin's 1990 law says only that a long online argument is likely to produce a comparison to Hitler or the Nazis. The rule that whoever makes the comparison loses was added later by the Usenet community, not by Godwin.

Tell someone: Godwin's 1990 law says only that a long online argument is likely to produce a Hitler comparison; the loser rule came later, from Usenet.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version treats the "loser" rule as part of Godwin's law: whoever invokes Hitler ends the argument and loses it.

## What's the source?

- [R Street](https://www.rstreet.org/commentary/i-created-godwins-law-in-1990-but-it-wasnt-a-prediction-it-was-a-warning/)

# Did habeas corpus come from Magna Carta?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Habeas corpus did not come from Magna Carta. Its roots predate the charter of 1215. It grew out of English common law over centuries, and the Habeas Corpus Act of 1679 codified it.

# Did Hardin later admit the tragedy of the commons was missing a word?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** Garrett Hardin later conceded that his error had been to omit one word: "unmanaged." His tragedy describes an unmanaged, open-access resource, not every shared one.

Tell someone: Garrett Hardin later conceded his famous essay left out one word, "unmanaged," and Elinor Ostrom documented communities that manage shared resources successfully.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version treats the tragedy as an iron law: any resource held in common will be ruined unless it is privatized or controlled by the state.

# Did Harvard Business Review reject Conway's law?

> Did Harvard Business Review reject Conway's law? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-harvard-business-review-reject-conways-law.html

Story No. 77 · [Round 8: Jokes that became laws](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-08.html)

# Did *Harvard Business Review* reject Conway's law?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** By Melvin Conway's own account, *Harvard Business Review* rejected his paper on the grounds that he had not proved his thesis. "How Do Committees Invent?" appeared instead in *Datamation* in April 1968.

Tell someone: By Melvin Conway's own account, *Harvard Business Review* rejected the paper behind his law as unproved; the evidence that it was right came decades later.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular assumption is that a law now quoted so widely in management and software circles must have arrived through a leading management journal.

## What's the source?

- [Conway, "Conway's Law"](https://www.melconway.com/Home/Conways_Law.html)
- [Conway, "How Do Committees Invent?"](https://www.melconway.com/Home/Committees_Paper.html)
- ["Conway's law," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conway%27s_law)

# Did Hawthorne factory output rise whatever the lighting?

> Did Hawthorne factory output rise whatever the lighting? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-hawthorne-factory-output-rise-whatever-the-lighting.html

Story No. 23 · [Round 3: Famous experiments, retold](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-03.html)

# Did Hawthorne factory output rise whatever the lighting?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The original Hawthorne lighting data do not show output rising whatever the lighting. When Steven Levitt and John List reanalyzed them, they called the famous patterns "entirely fictional".

Tell someone: When Levitt and List reopened the original Hawthorne lighting records, they called the famous output patterns "entirely fictional".

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is a neat paradox. At a factory in the 1920s, researchers brightened the lights and output rose. They dimmed the lights and output rose again. The conclusion drawn was that the workers were responding to the attention of being studied, not to the lighting.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [NBER w15016](https://www.nber.org/papers/w15016)
- ["Hawthorne effect," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawthorne_effect)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Levitt & List, "Was There Really a Hawthorne Effect at the Hawthorne Plant?" *American Economic Journal: Applied Economics* 3(1) (2011; NBER w15016, 2009). "Hawthorne effect," Wikipedia. "Hawthorne Effect," Simply Psychology. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/hawthorne-effect/).

# Did Hebb say "neurons that fire together wire together"?

> Did Hebb say "neurons that fire together wire together"? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-hebb-say-neurons-that-fire-together-wire-together.html

Story No. 12 · [Round 2: Who really said it?](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-02.html)

# Did Hebb say "neurons that fire together wire together"?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Donald Hebb set out the rule in 1949. The slogan is not his. It came in 1992, usually credited to Carla Shatz as a mnemonic, and crediting it to Hebb is, in the record's words, the most common error about the rule.

Tell someone: Hebb set out his rule in 1949, but the rhyme "fire together, wire together" came in 1992 and is usually credited to Carla Shatz.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version puts the rhyme in Hebb's mouth, as his own summary of how learning works in the brain.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Language Log, "Firing and wiring"](https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=25194)
- ["Hebbian theory," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebbian_theory)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Hebb, *The Organization of Behavior* (1949; reissued 2005). "Donald Olding Hebb," Canadian Association for Neuroscience. "Hebbian theory," ScienceDirect Topics. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/hebbs-rule/).

# Did Henry Kissinger say academic politics are vicious because the stakes are so small?

> Did Henry Kissinger say academic politics are vicious because the stakes are so small? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-henry-kissinger-say-academic-politics-are-vicious-because-the-stakes-are-so-small.html

Story No. 20 · [Round 2: Who really said it?](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-02.html)

# Did Henry Kissinger say academic politics are vicious because the stakes are so small?

Just show me the answer

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** The line has been credited to Henry Kissinger, but he is one of several claimants, and none has a clean title. The record calls the attribution famously tangled. Its usual namesake is the Columbia political scientist Wallace Sayre, and Quote Investigator traces the idea back to Samuel Johnson in 1765.

Tell someone: Kissinger is only one claimant to the academic-politics quip; Quote Investigator traces the idea back to Samuel Johnson in 1765.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is a Kissinger line: academic politics are so vicious because the stakes are so small.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Quote Investigator](https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/08/18/acad-politics/)
- ["Sayre's law," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sayre%27s_law)

# Did Hooke publish his law as an anagram?

> Did Hooke publish his law as an anagram? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-hooke-publish-his-law-as-an-anagram.html

Story No. 89 · [Round 9: Discovery stories](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-09.html)

# Did Hooke publish his law as an anagram?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** Robert Hooke published his law of springs in 1676 as the anagram "ceiiinosssttuu." In 1678 he revealed the answer: "ut tensio, sic vis," as the extension, so the force.

Tell someone: Hooke published his spring law in 1676 as the anagram "ceiiinosssttuu," and only revealed in 1678 that it spelled "ut tensio, sic vis."

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version assumes nothing of the sort. A law taught as a single line of algebra is presumed to have been published plainly, like any other result.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Hooke, *Lectiones Cutlerianae* (1679), containing *De Potentia Restitutiva*, EarlyPrint text](https://distantreader.org/stacks/earlyprint/txt/A44320.txt)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Hooke, *Lectures de Potentia Restitutiva, or of Spring* (1678). "Hooke's law," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/hookes-law/).

# Did Kelly Johnson coin "Keep it simple, stupid"?

> Did Kelly Johnson coin "Keep it simple, stupid"? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-kelly-johnson-coin-keep-it-simple-stupid.html

Story No. 79 · [Round 8: Jokes that became laws](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-08.html)

# Did Kelly Johnson coin "Keep it simple, stupid"?

Just show me the answer

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** The phrase is attributed to Kelly Johnson, lead engineer at Lockheed's Skunk Works, but the attribution is not airtight. A 1938 *Minneapolis Star* article used the variant "keep it short and simple," before Johnson's association with the phrase, and the earliest dated record of the acronym itself is a U.S. Navy "Project KISS" in 1960.

Tell someone: KISS is attributed to Kelly Johnson, but a 1938 newspaper already used "keep it short and simple," so who said it first is not settled.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version credits Johnson alone, the engineer who coined KISS.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Rich, NAS memoir](https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/johnson-clarence.pdf)
- ["KISS principle," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KISS_principle)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: "KISS principle," Wikipedia. Rich, *Clarence Leonard (Kelly) Johnson 1910–1990: A Biographical Memoir*, National Academy of Sciences (1995). The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/kiss-principle/).

# Did Marilyn vos Savant's correct Monty Hall answer draw a storm of objections?

> Did Marilyn vos Savant's correct Monty Hall answer draw a storm of objections? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-marilyn-vos-savants-correct-monty-hall-answer-draw-a-storm-of-objections.html

Story No. 40 · [Round 4: Charts and numbers](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-04.html)

# Did Marilyn vos Savant's correct Monty Hall answer draw a storm of objections?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** When Marilyn vos Savant gave the correct answer to the Monty Hall problem in 1990, some ten thousand readers wrote in, close to a thousand of them with doctorates, insisting she was wrong.

Tell someone: By her own estimate, some ten thousand readers, close to a thousand with doctorates, wrote in to tell Marilyn vos Savant she was wrong, and she was right.

## What's the version people tell?

The story is told as a parable of expert overconfidence. A columnist got a probability puzzle right, and thousands of readers, many with advanced degrees, told her she had got it wrong. It sounds too neat to be true.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- ["Monty Hall problem," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monty_Hall_problem)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Selvin, letters to *The American Statistician* (1975). Tierney, "Behind Monty Hall's Doors: Puzzle, Debate and Answer?" *The New York Times* (1991). "The Time Everyone 'Corrected' the World's Smartest Woman," Priceonomics. "Monty Hall problem," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/the-monty-hall-problem/).

# Did Mark Twain say "If all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail"?

> Did Mark Twain say "If all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail"? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-mark-twain-say-if-all-you-have-is-a-hammer-everything-looks-like-a-nail.html

Story No. 13 · [Round 2: Who really said it?](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-02.html)

# Did Mark Twain say "If all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail"?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** There is no evidence that Mark Twain said it. The idea was named by the philosopher Abraham Kaplan in 1964, after a talk in 1962. Its best-known hammer-and-nail form is Abraham Maslow's, from 1966.

Tell someone: There is no evidence Twain said it: Abraham Kaplan named the law of the instrument in 1964, and Maslow's hammer-and-nail version followed in 1966.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is a Twain quip about the habit of using the one tool a person knows for every job.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Quote Investigator](https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/05/08/hammer-nail/)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: "If Your Only Tool Is a Hammer Then Every Problem Looks Like a Nail," Quote Investigator (2014). "Law of the instrument," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/the-law-of-the-instrument/).

# Did Maslow draw the pyramid of needs?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Maslow did not draw the pyramid. The famous diagram was created by later authors, not by Maslow himself.

Tell someone: The hierarchy of needs is Maslow's, but the pyramid came from later authors, and his own ordering was less rigid than the shape.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is a five-tier pyramid credited to Abraham Maslow, with physiological needs at the base and self-actualization at the tip, each layer to be completed before the next.

# Did Maxwell write the four Maxwell's equations?

> Did Maxwell write the four Maxwell's equations? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-maxwell-write-the-four-maxwells-equations.html

Story No. 42 · [Round 5: Names that mislead](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-05.html)

# Did Maxwell write the four Maxwell's equations?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** James Clerk Maxwell built the theory, but the four compact equations that carry his name are Oliver Heaviside's reformulation of 1884. Maxwell's own 1865 paper contained twenty equations.

Tell someone: Maxwell built the theory, but his 1865 paper had twenty equations; Oliver Heaviside condensed them into the famous four in 1884.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version holds that Maxwell wrote down the four equations taught today, in the vector form printed in textbooks.

# Did Mendeleev invent the periodic table alone?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Dmitri Mendeleev published his periodic table in 1869, but he did not conceive it alone. John Newlands had proposed a related law of octaves in 1865, and Julius Lothar Meyer worked out a similar arrangement independently at about the same time.

The popular version gives the table to one man in one year: Mendeleev, 1869.

# Did Milgram prove we are all six handshakes apart?

> Did Milgram prove we are all six handshakes apart? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-milgram-prove-we-are-all-six-handshakes-apart.html

Story No. 25 · [Round 3: Famous experiments, retold](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-03.html)

# Did Milgram prove we are all six handshakes apart?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Milgram did not prove that everyone is six handshakes apart. Most of the chains in his 1967 experiment never reached their target, and the "six" is a median over the minority that did.

Tell someone: Most of the chains in Milgram's small-world experiment never reached their target, and the famous six is a median of the minority that did.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version credits "six degrees of separation" to a single experiment. Stanley Milgram, it says, showed that any two people are linked by six acquaintances.

## What's the source?

Cited in the book: Karinthy, "Chains" (1929). Milgram, "The Small World Problem," *Psychology Today* (May 1967). Travers & Milgram, "An Experimental Study of the Small World Problem," *Sociometry* 32 (1969). Kleinfeld, "The Small World Problem," *Society* 39(2) (2002). Watts & Strogatz, *Nature* 393 (1998). "Small-world experiment," Wikipedia. Backstrom et al., "Four Degrees of Separation" (2012), arXiv:1111.4570. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/the-small-world-phenomenon/).

# Did more efficient steam engines make Britain burn more coal?

> Did more efficient steam engines make Britain burn more coal? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-more-efficient-steam-engines-make-britain-burn-more-coal.html

Story No. 93 · [Round 10: Money, power and policy](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-10.html)

# Did more efficient steam engines make Britain burn more coal?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** In *The Coal Question* (1865), the economist William Stanley Jevons observed that England's coal use soared after more efficient steam engines expanded coal's industrial uses.

Tell someone: Jevons observed in 1865 that more efficient steam engines made coal cheaper to use, so Britain found new uses and burned more of it.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is an assumption rather than a story. A more efficient engine burns less coal for each job, so a country with better engines should burn less coal.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Jevons, *The Coal Question* (1865), Internet Archive full text](https://archive.org/stream/coalquestionani00jevogoog/coalquestionani00jevogoog_djvu.txt)

# Did Napoleon say "Never attribute to malice what can be explained by stupidity"?

> Did Napoleon say "Never attribute to malice what can be explained by stupidity"? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-napoleon-say-never-attribute-to-malice-what-can-be-explained-by-stupidity.html

Story No. 16 · [Round 2: Who really said it?](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-02.html)

# Did Napoleon say "Never attribute to malice what can be explained by stupidity"?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The line is not Napoleon's. Quote Investigator, the source the record cites for its dated history of the saying, debunks the Napoleon attribution. The earliest known printing of the razor is from 1980.

Tell someone: The line is not Napoleon's: the razor's first known printing is Arthur Bloch's 1980 book, with a close version in Heinlein from 1941.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version attaches the warning against blaming malice for what stupidity explains to Napoleon.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Quote Investigator](https://quoteinvestigator.com/2016/12/30/not-malice/)
- ["Hanlon's razor," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanlon%27s_razor)

# Did Newton himself tell the apple story?

TRUE

Just show me the answer

**True.** The apple story is not a fable invented by Newton's admirers. According to *Encyclopaedia Britannica*, it traces back to Newton's own later recollection. Only the apple hitting his head was added afterward.

Tell someone: Newton himself told of the apple, according to *Britannica*; only the bump on the head was added later.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version here is a skeptic's one. The apple, it says, is pure myth: a tidy tale invented by later admirers to dress his work in a moment of genius.

# Did Parkinson's law begin as a joke in The Economist?

> Did Parkinson's law begin as a joke in The Economist? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-parkinsons-law-begin-as-a-joke-in-the-economist.html

Story No. 71 · [Round 8: Jokes that became laws](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-08.html)

# Did Parkinson's law begin as a joke in *The Economist*?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** Parkinson's law began as satire. The naval historian C. Northcote Parkinson opened a satirical essay in *The Economist* on 19 November 1955 with the "commonplace observation" that made his name: work "expands so as to fill the time available for its completion."

Tell someone: Parkinson's law began as a 1955 satirical essay in *The Economist* about an Admiralty whose bureaucracy grew as its fleet shrank.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version treats it as a management finding, a rule distilled from research into how organizations work.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- ["Parkinson's law," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkinson%27s_law)
- ["Law of triviality," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_triviality)

# Did Philippa Foot invent the trolley problem?

Story No. 83 · [Round 9: Discovery stories](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-09.html)

# Did Philippa Foot invent the trolley problem?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** Philippa Foot introduced the original case in 1967, in a paper called "The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of the Double Effect." She did not name it. Judith Jarvis Thomson called it the trolley problem and added its best-known variants in 1976 and 1985.

Tell someone: Philippa Foot set out the trolley case in 1967, but the name belongs to Judith Jarvis Thomson, who also added the footbridge variant.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version comes in two forms. One treats the puzzle as an old one, too old to trace. The other treats it as a modern psychology test.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- ["Trolley problem," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trolley_problem)
- ["Doctrine of Double Effect," SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/double-effect/)

# Did Pythagoras discover the Pythagorean theorem?

![Cartoon for the question: Did Pythagoras discover the Pythagorean theorem?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/005.png)

FOLKLORE

Just show me the answer

**Folklore.** The relation that carries Pythagoras's name was known and used long before him. A Babylonian tablet from around 1800 BC lists its number triples, and Pythagoras lived from about 570 to 495 BC.

Tell someone: A Babylonian tablet from around 1800 BC already lists Pythagorean triples, more than a thousand years before Pythagoras was born.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is simple. Pythagoras of Samos discovered that in a right triangle the square on the longest side equals the sum of the squares on the other two, and the theorem is named after him for that reason.

## What's the source?

- ["Plimpton 322," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plimpton_322)

# Did Say write "supply creates its own demand"?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The phrase "supply creates its own demand" does not appear in Jean-Baptiste Say's own writing. John Maynard Keynes popularized it in 1936, and even Keynes seems to have been quoting a phrase already current.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version treats the slogan as Say's law in Say's words: a French economist's claim that whatever is produced will find a buyer.

# Did Stigler credit Stigler's law to someone else?

> Did Stigler credit Stigler's law to someone else? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-stigler-credit-stiglers-law-to-someone-else.html

Story No. 41 · [Round 5: Names that mislead](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-05.html)

# Did Stigler credit Stigler's law to someone else?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** In the 1980 paper that named the law after himself, the statistician Stephen Stigler credited its discovery to the sociologist Robert K. Merton. The law says no scientific discovery is named after its original discoverer, so it was built to obey itself.

Tell someone: Stigler named Stigler's law after himself and then credited its discovery to Robert K. Merton, so the law obeys itself.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular assumption is the natural one. A law with a person's name on it was found by that person, and Stigler's law of eponymy belongs to Stigler.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- ["Stigler's law of eponymy," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stigler%27s_law_of_eponymy)

Merton* (1980). "Stigler's law of eponymy," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/stiglers-law/).

# Did Sturgeon say "Ninety percent of everything is crap"?

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Theodore Sturgeon's printed word was "crud," not "crap." His *Venture Science Fiction* column first printed it in September 1957. In March 1958 the column gave it as "Ninety percent of everything is crud." He also called it his Revelation, not his law.

The popular version quotes Sturgeon's law in a blunter word: "Ninety percent of everything is crap."

# Did the Stanford prison guards turn cruel on their own?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The guards did not become cruel on their own. Archival recordings and later scholarship show that the experimenters, including the warden, instructed and pressured them to be tough.

Tell someone: Archival recordings show the Stanford prison guards were instructed and pressured to be tough, which Thibault Le Texier argues made the abuse substantially coached.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version runs as follows. In 1971 ordinary students at Stanford were given guard uniforms and authority over fellow students playing prisoners, and within days they turned abusive without being told to. The lesson drawn is that a bad situation can make anyone cruel.

# Did the Sydney Opera House open a decade late and vastly over budget?

> Did the Sydney Opera House open a decade late and vastly over budget? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-the-sydney-opera-house-open-a-decade-late-and-vastly-over-budget.html

Story No. 98 · [Round 10: Money, power and policy](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-10.html)

# Did the Sydney Opera House open a decade late and vastly over budget?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** The Sydney Opera House was estimated to open in 1963 at a cost of a few million pounds. A scaled-down version opened in 1973 at A$102 million. The exact figures vary by source.

Tell someone: The Sydney Opera House opened a decade late, in 1973, scaled down and costing more than a hundred million, though exact figures vary by source.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version holds the Opera House up as the classic runaway project. Famous stories of waste tend to grow in the retelling, so it is fair to suspect this one has too.

## What's the source?

- [Flyvbjerg et al. (2002), arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.6604)

# Did Thomas Gresham formulate Gresham's law?

> Did Thomas Gresham formulate Gresham's law? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-thomas-gresham-formulate-greshams-law.html

Story No. 44 · [Round 5: Names that mislead](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-05.html)

# Did Thomas Gresham formulate Gresham's law?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Thomas Gresham did not formulate Gresham's law. Henry Dunning Macleod named it after him in 1858, and the principle had been stated long before: by Oresme, by Copernicus around 1519, and in Aristophanes' play *The Frogs* around 405 BC.

Tell someone: Gresham did not formulate Gresham's law; Macleod named it after him in 1858, and Aristophanes stated the principle around 405 BC.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version credits Gresham, a Tudor financier, with the observation that bad money drives out good.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Selgin, "Gresham's Law," EH.Net](https://eh.net/encyclopedia/greshams-law/)
- ["Sir Thomas Gresham," History of Economic Thought](https://hetwebsite.net/het/profiles/gresham.htm)
- [Mainelli, "Sir Thomas Gresham: Tudor, Trader, Shipper, Spy"](https://www.mainelli.org/?p=1497)
- ["Gresham's law," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gresham%27s_law)
- ["Coinage Act of 1965," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coinage_Act_of_1965)

# Did Thomas Young shine light through two slits?

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** Thomas Young showed that light interferes, in his Bakerian Lectures around 1801 and 1803. Whether he performed a literal two-slit experiment is disputed: his demonstrations used sunlight, pinholes and narrow cards.

The popular version has Young shining light through two slits around 1801, seeing bands on a screen and proving that light is a wave.

# Did Wald really tell the military to armor where returning planes weren't hit?

> Did Wald really tell the military to armor where returning planes weren't hit? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-wald-really-tell-the-military-to-armor-where-returning-planes-werent-hit.html

Story No. 36 · [Round 4: Charts and numbers](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-04.html)

# Did Wald really tell the military to armor where returning planes weren't hit?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** The reasoning in the famous story is Wald's. In his 1943 memoranda he estimated aircraft vulnerability from the damage on returning planes, while accounting for the planes that did not return.

Tell someone: Wald did reason that armor belongs where returning planes had the fewest bullet holes, since planes hit there did not come back.

## What's the version people tell?

The story is so neat that it is easy to doubt. A statistician looks at bombers riddled with holes and says to armor the places with no holes, because planes hit there never made it home. It sounds like a parable invented to teach a point.

## What's the source?

Cited in the book: Wald, "A Method of Estimating Plane Vulnerability Based on Damage of Survivors" (1943; Center for Naval Analyses reprint, 1980). Wallis, "The Statistical Research Group, 1942–1945: Rejoinder," *Journal of the American Statistical Association* 75 (1980). Elton, Gruber & Blake, "Survivorship Bias and Mutual Fund Performance," *Review of Financial Studies* 9(4) (1996). "Survivorship bias," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/survivorship-bias/).

# Did Weber write "iron cage"?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Max Weber did not write "iron cage." The English phrase is Talcott Parsons's 1930 translation of Weber's German *stahlhartes Gehäuse*, which more literally means a shell or casing as hard as steel.

# Did William of Ockham write "Entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity"?

> Did William of Ockham write "Entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity"? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/did-william-of-ockham-write-entities-should-not-be-multiplied-beyond-necessity.html

Story No. 11 · [Round 2: Who really said it?](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-02.html)

# Did William of Ockham write "Entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity"?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The famous Latin sentence is nowhere in Ockham's surviving works. Its earliest close version was written by John Punch in 1639, nearly three centuries after Ockham died. Ockham argued for the same principle, in other words.

Tell someone: The famous Latin line of Occam's razor is not in Ockham's works; John Punch wrote a close version in 1639, nearly three centuries after Ockham died.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is that the medieval friar William of Ockham wrote *Entia non sunt multiplicanda praeter necessitatem*, "entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity," and so gave his name to the razor.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- ["William of Ockham," SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/ockham/)
- ["Who sharpened Occam's Razor?," Irish Philosophy, archived](https://web.archive.org/web/2022/https://www.irishphilosophy.com/2014/05/27/who-sharpened-occams-razor/)
- ["Occam's razor," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occam%27s_razor)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Ockham, *Summa Logicae*, part I, ch. 12. "Occam's razor," Wikipedia. Baker, "Simplicity," *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy* (rev. 2022). The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/occams-razor/).

# Do the least skilled people really overrate themselves the most?

> Do the least skilled people really overrate themselves the most? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/do-the-least-skilled-people-really-overrate-themselves-the-most.html

Story No. 32 · [Round 4: Charts and numbers](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-04.html)

# Do the least skilled people really overrate themselves the most?

Just show me the answer

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** In 1999 Kruger and Dunning found that the lowest scorers on several tests overestimated their rank. Since 2016 several researchers have argued that much of that pattern is a statistical artifact, and a 2026 reanalysis reports that it inverts.

Tell someone: The 1999 finding that low scorers overrated their rank is disputed, and a 2026 reanalysis reports overconfidence was most pronounced among the highest performers.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is blunter than the paper. The incompetent, it says, are too incompetent to know it, while experts underrate themselves. In its shortest form: stupid people think they are geniuses.

## What's the source?

- [Gignac & Zajenkowski abstract via Semantic Scholar](https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/DOI:10.1016/j.intell.2020.101449)

- [Kruger & Dunning 1999](https://holub.com/goodies/incompetence.pdf)

# Does a broken bone heal back stronger?

> Does a broken bone heal back stronger? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/does-a-broken-bone-heal-back-stronger.html

Story No. 58 · [Round 6: Physics in the kitchen and the sky](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-06.html)

# Does a broken bone heal back stronger?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** There is no evidence, contrary to popular belief, that a healed fracture becomes stronger than the original unbroken bone. The claim is an overstatement of Wolff's law, which describes how healthy bone adapts to the loads placed on it.

Tell someone: No evidence shows a healed fracture becomes stronger than the original bone; healthy bone instead adapts to the loads it carries.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version holds that a bone knits back stronger at the break than it was before.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- ["Wolff's law," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolff%27s_law)
- [McGill OSS](https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/node/7026)
- [Hackensack Meridian Health, "Do Broken Bones Heal Stronger?"](https://www.hackensackmeridianhealth.org/HealthU/2021/08/02/do-broken-bones-heal-stronger)
- [*EFORT Open Reviews* 3 (2018), doi:10.1302/2058-5241.3.170024, copy at](https://rcastoragev2.blob.core.windows.net/bfc04c3db6004083d7570820e4c2f20d/PMC5890130.pdf)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: "Wolff's law," Wikipedia. Modern review on bone functional adaptation, PMC. McVean, "Broken Bones Grow Back Stronger… Sort Of," McGill Office for Science and Society (2018). "Long-term bone remodelling around 'legendary' cementless femoral stems," *EFORT Open Reviews* 3 (2018). The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/wolffs-law/).

# Does air over a wing speed up to meet the air underneath?

> Does air over a wing speed up to meet the air underneath? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/does-air-over-a-wing-speed-up-to-meet-the-air-underneath.html

Story No. 56 · [Round 6: Physics in the kitchen and the sky](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-06.html)

# Does air over a wing speed up to meet the air underneath?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Air does move faster over a wing's upper surface, and the pressure there is lower. But the popular reason, that the air must hurry to rejoin the air beneath, is a misconception that NASA debunks.

Tell someone: NASA debunks the equal-transit-time story, yet air over a wing does move faster and at lower pressure, and Bernoulli's principle does contribute to lift.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is the "equal transit time" story. The upper surface of a wing is longer, so air passing over it must speed up to meet the air passing underneath at the back of the wing. Faster air means lower pressure, and the wing is lifted.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [NASA Glenn, "Incorrect Lift Theory"](https://www.grc.nasa.gov/WWW/K-12/VirtualAero/BottleRocket/airplane/wrong1.html)
- [NASA Glenn, "Lift," updated July 11, 2024](https://www1.grc.nasa.gov/beginners-guide-to-aeronautics/lift-3/)
- ["Bernoulli's principle," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernoulli%27s_principle)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: NASA Glenn Research Center (Tom Benson), "Incorrect Lift Theory." "Bernoulli's principle," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/bernoullis-principle/).

# Does hot water freeze faster than cold?

> Does hot water freeze faster than cold? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/does-hot-water-freeze-faster-than-cold.html

Story No. 57 · [Round 6: Physics in the kitchen and the sky](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-06.html)

# Does hot water freeze faster than cold?

Just show me the answer

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** Whether hot water can freeze faster than cold is unresolved. Erasto Mpemba and Denis Osborne published the claim in 1969, a careful 2016 study by Burridge and Linden found no evidence for a meaningful effect, and the record says the dispute remains open.

Tell someone: A careful 2016 study found no evidence for a meaningful Mpemba effect, but whether hot water can freeze faster remains unresolved.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is simple: hot water freezes first, and the effect carries Mpemba's name.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Burridge & Linden 2016, PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5121640)
- ["Mpemba effect," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mpemba_effect)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Mpemba & Osborne, "Cool?," *Physics Education* 4 (1969). Burridge & Linden, "Questioning the Mpemba effect," *Scientific Reports* 6 (2016). "Mpemba effect," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/mpemba-effect/).

# Does Laffer himself say the Laffer curve wasn't his idea?

> Does Laffer himself say the Laffer curve wasn't his idea? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Story No. 47 · [Round 5: Names that mislead](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-05.html)

# Does Laffer himself say the Laffer curve wasn't his idea?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** Arthur Laffer has disclaimed originality for the curve that bears his name. He credits earlier sources, including Ibn Khaldun in the fourteenth century and John Maynard Keynes.

Tell someone: Arthur Laffer has disclaimed originality for the Laffer curve, crediting earlier sources including Ibn Khaldun in the fourteenth century and John Maynard Keynes.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version makes Laffer the inventor of the idea that cutting taxes can raise revenue.

## What's the source?

# Does "red herring" come from training hounds with smoked fish?

> Does "red herring" come from training hounds with smoked fish? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/does-red-herring-come-from-training-hounds-with-smoked-fish.html

Story No. 61 · [Round 7: Words and phrases](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-07.html)

# Does "red herring" come from training hounds with smoked fish?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The hound-training origin is likely a myth. The figurative sense of "red herring" is real, and it is traceable to the journalist William Cobbett in 1807.

Tell someone: The hound-training story is likely a myth; the figurative "red herring" traces to the journalist William Cobbett in 1807.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version explains the phrase with a scene from the hunting field. Hunters, it says, dragged a strong-smelling smoked fish across a trail, either to train their hounds or to throw them off a scent. A red herring, on this account, is whatever pulls the dogs away from the trail they should be following.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Quinion, World Wide Words](https://www.worldwidewords.org/articles/herring.htm)
- ["Red herring," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_herring)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Quinion, "The Lure of the Red Herring," World Wide Words (2008). "Red herring," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/the-red-herring/).

# Does the Coriolis effect decide which way a sink drains?

> Does the Coriolis effect decide which way a sink drains? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/does-the-coriolis-effect-decide-which-way-a-sink-drains.html

Story No. 52 · [Round 6: Physics in the kitchen and the sky](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-06.html)

# Does the Coriolis effect decide which way a sink drains?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** At the scale of a sink, bath or toilet, the Coriolis effect is thousands of times too weak to set the direction of draining. Water drains both ways within the same hemisphere.

Tell someone: The Coriolis effect is thousands of times too weak to set a sink's draining direction, so water drains both ways in either hemisphere.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version says the Earth's rotation makes water swirl down drains one way in the Northern Hemisphere and the other way in the Southern.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- ["Coriolis force," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coriolis_force)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: "Coriolis force," Wikipedia. "Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis," *Encyclopaedia Britannica*. Shapiro, "Bath-Tub Vortex," *Nature* 196 (1962). Trefethen et al., "The Bath-Tub Vortex in the Southern Hemisphere," *Nature* 207 (1965). The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/coriolis-effect/).
