# Does waiting for a second marshmallow predict success in life?

> Does waiting for a second marshmallow predict success in life? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/does-waiting-for-a-second-marshmallow-predict-success-in-life.html

Story No. 27 · [Round 3: Famous experiments, retold](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-03.html)

# Does waiting for a second marshmallow predict success in life?

Just show me the answer

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** Early follow-ups linked a preschooler's ability to wait with later achievement. A larger 2018 replication found the link much weaker and largely explained by family background.

Tell someone: Waiting for a second marshmallow tracked later achievement in small early samples, but a larger 2018 study found the link largely explained by family background.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is a parable about willpower. Children who could wait for a second marshmallow, it says, grew into more successful adults, so self-control at four predicts success in life.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Watts, Duncan & Quan 2018 abstract via Europe PMC](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=DOI:10.1177/0956797618761661)
- [sample sizes from Conversable Economist](https://conversableeconomist.com/2018/06/04/the-not-so-triumphant-return-of-the-marshmallow-test/)
- ["Stanford marshmallow experiment," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_marshmallow_experiment)
- [Michaelson & Munakata 2020](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/73c9d031)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Shoda, Mischel & Peake, *Developmental Psychology* (1990). Watts, Duncan & Quan, "Revisiting the Marshmallow Test," *Psychological Science* 29(7) (2018). "Stanford marshmallow experiment," Wikipedia. "Marshmallow test," *Encyclopaedia Britannica*. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/the-marshmallow-test/).

The editor

# Krishna Chagti

Founder of Conyso and editor of Conyso Publishing's books.

## What does the editor do?

Krishna Chagti founded Conyso, which publishes [the Law Tome](https://conyso.com/lawtome/) and [the Bias Atlas](https://conyso.com/biases/) as free, sourced datasets. He edits the books built from them.

Editing here means deciding what goes in and standing behind what the book says. The text is drafted with AI from the sourced records. Every verdict, quote and date is then checked against a primary source, or the best one available, and the check is logged. A story whose verdict is still open waits until it is settled. The illustrations are made with AI. Mistakes found after print go on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

# Has toast landing butter-side down been studied seriously?

> Has toast landing butter-side down been studied seriously? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/has-toast-landing-butter-side-down-been-studied-seriously.html

Story No. 76 · [Round 8: Jokes that became laws](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-08.html)

# Has toast landing butter-side down been studied seriously?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** In 1995 the physicist Robert Matthews published "Tumbling toast, Murphy's Law and the fundamental constants" in the *European Journal of Physics*. It won a 1996 Ig Nobel Prize, and it argued that toast does tend to land butter-side down, for mundane physical reasons.

Tell someone: A 1995 physics paper argued that toast dropped from table height rotates only about half a turn, so it tends to land butter-side down.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version treats falling toast as a joke about bad luck with no science behind it, the emblem of Sod's law.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Ig Nobel winners, improbable.com](https://improbable.com/ig/winners/)
- ["Buttered toast phenomenon," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buttered_toast_phenomenon)
- ["Sod's law," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sod%27s_law)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Matthews, "Tumbling toast, Murphy's Law and the fundamental constants," *European Journal of Physics* 16(4): 172-176 (1995). Ig Nobel Prize, Physics (1996), improbable.com. "Buttered toast phenomenon," Wikipedia. "Sod's law," Wikipedia. "Sod's law," *Collins English Dictionary*. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/sods-law/).

# True, folklore or disputed?

Conyso Publishing makes quiz and reference books from the Law Tome's sourced records. Guess first. Then find out what actually happened.

48 FOLKLORE · 34 TRUE · 18 DISPUTED

![Cartoon for the question: Did an apple fall on Newton's head?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/002.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 2

### [Did an apple fall on Newton's head?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-an-apple-fall-on-newtons-head.html)

**Folklore.** There is an apple in Newton's own account of his thinking about gravity. It does not hit him on the head. That detail is a later embellishment.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-an-apple-fall-on-newtons-head.html)

## You've heard these. Which ones happened?

Your score

–

Make a call to start

![Cartoon for the question: Did Archimedes shout "Eureka!" in the bath?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/001.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 1

### [Did Archimedes shout "Eureka!" in the bath?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-archimedes-shout-eureka-in-the-bath.html)

**Folklore.** Archimedes stated the law of buoyancy around 250 BC, in his treatise *On Floating Bodies*. The bath, the crown and the cry of "Eureka!" are almost certainly a later embellishment.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-archimedes-shout-eureka-in-the-bath.html)

![Cartoon for the question: Did Newton himself tell the apple story?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/003.png)

TRUE

Round 1 · No. 3

### [Did Newton himself tell the apple story?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-newton-himself-tell-the-apple-story.html)

**True.** The apple story is not a fable invented by Newton's admirers. According to *Encyclopaedia Britannica*, it traces back to Newton's own later recollection. Only the apple hitting his head was added afterward.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-newton-himself-tell-the-apple-story.html)

![Cartoon for the question: Did Galileo drop balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/004.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 4

### [Did Galileo drop balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-galileo-drop-balls-from-the-leaning-tower-of-pisa.html)

**Folklore.** The tower drop is likely a legend. It is not in Galileo's own writings. His documented work on falling bodies used balls rolling down ramps, with notes from around 1603 to 1604 and results published in 1638.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-galileo-drop-balls-from-the-leaning-tower-of-pisa.html)

![Cartoon for the question: Did Pythagoras discover the Pythagorean theorem?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/005.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 5

### [Did Pythagoras discover the Pythagorean theorem?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-pythagoras-discover-the-pythagorean-theorem.html)

**Folklore.** The relation that carries Pythagoras's name was known and used long before him. A Babylonian tablet from around 1800 BC lists its number triples, and Pythagoras lived from about 570 to 495 BC.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-pythagoras-discover-the-pythagorean-theorem.html)

![Cartoon for the question: Did Einstein write E = mc² in his 1905 paper?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/006.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 6

### [Did Einstein write E = mc² in his 1905 paper?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-einstein-write-e-mc2-in-his-1905-paper.html)

**Folklore.** Einstein's 1905 paper contains the idea but not the famous formula. It states in a single sentence that a body which gives off energy as radiation loses mass in proportion.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-einstein-write-e-mc2-in-his-1905-paper.html)

![Cartoon for the question: Did Einstein win his Nobel Prize for something other than relativity?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/007.png)

TRUE

Round 1 · No. 7

### [Did Einstein win his Nobel Prize for something other than relativity?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-einstein-win-his-nobel-prize-for-something-other-than-relativity.html)

**True.** Einstein's Nobel Prize, the physics prize designated for 1921, was for his work on the photoelectric effect. NobelPrize.org gives the citation as "for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect." Relativity is not what the prize named.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-einstein-win-his-nobel-prize-for-something-other-than-relativity.html)

![Cartoon for the question: Did Gordon Moore say chips double every 18 months?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/008.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 8

### [Did Gordon Moore say chips double every 18 months?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-gordon-moore-say-chips-double-every-18-months.html)

**Folklore.** Gordon Moore never gave 18 months. His 1965 article predicted that the number of components on a chip would double roughly every year, and in 1975 he revised that to every two years.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-gordon-moore-say-chips-double-every-18-months.html)

![Cartoon for the question: Did Churchill promise "blood, sweat and tears"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/009.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 9

### [Did Churchill promise "blood, sweat and tears"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-churchill-promise-blood-sweat-and-tears.html)

**Folklore.** In May 1940 Churchill offered "blood, toil, tears and sweat." That is four items, not three, and "toil" is the word that dropped out.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-churchill-promise-blood-sweat-and-tears.html)

![Cartoon for the question: Did Edward Murphy say "Anything that can go wrong will go wrong"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/010.png)

DISPUTED

Round 1 · No. 10

### [Did Edward Murphy say "Anything that can go wrong will go wrong"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-edward-murphy-say-anything-that-can-go-wrong-will-go-wrong.html)

**Disputed.** A maxim like it came out of an Air Force rocket-sled project around 1949, and Murphy's name stuck to it. Who first said it, and in what words, is not settled. The earliest firm printing under Murphy's name, from 1952, credits an unnamed physicist.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-edward-murphy-say-anything-that-can-go-wrong-will-go-wrong.html)

[Play round 2: Who really said it? →](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-02.html) [See all ten rounds](https://conyso.com/publishing/true-or-folklore.html#rounds)

## Which series are there?

Series one

### The Law Tome

Named laws, effects and razors, and the stories told about them. Book 1, *True or Folklore?*, is coming soon.

Series two

### The Bias Atlas

Thinking errors, how to spot them and which findings held up. No titles announced yet.

## How are the books made?

1. **From a sourced record.** Each story starts from a Law Tome or Bias Atlas entry, which names its sources.
2. **Drafted with AI.** The text is drafted with AI from that record.
3. **Checked against the sources.** Every verdict, quote and date is checked against a primary source, or the best one available, and the check is logged on each story's page. A story whose verdict is still open waits.
4. **Illustrated with AI.** The cartoons are made with AI.
5. **Corrected in public.** Mistakes found after print go on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Edited by [Krishna Chagti](https://conyso.com/publishing/editor.html), the founder of Conyso. [His founder site](https://conyso.com/founder/) has the rest of his work.

## Questions people ask

What is Conyso Publishing?

Conyso's imprint for quiz and reference books. Each book is built from one of Conyso's free, sourced datasets: [the Law Tome](https://conyso.com/lawtome/) or [the Bias Atlas](https://conyso.com/biases/).

Is True or Folklore? out yet?

Not yet. It is coming soon in paperback and Kindle. This site will link to the store once it is on sale, and [the Law Tome's books page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/books/) shows its status.

Who writes the books? Is it AI?

The text is drafted with AI from the sourced records, then every verdict, quote and date is checked against a primary source, or the best one available. The illustrations are made with AI. [Krishna Chagti](https://conyso.com/publishing/editor.html) edits the books and signs off each one.

What does DISPUTED mean?

That the record is genuinely unsettled. Where good sources disagree, the book says so rather than picking a side.

What happens if a verdict is wrong?

It goes on the public [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/), with what changed.

Can I play the stories at a quiz night or in class?

Yes. The rounds on this site are free to play: read the question aloud, let everyone call it, then tap for the verdict. The book adds a two-team scoresheet and a page of classroom ideas.

# Is "Muphry's law" misspelled on purpose?

> Is "Muphry's law" misspelled on purpose? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/is-muphrys-law-misspelled-on-purpose.html

Story No. 50 · [Round 5: Names that mislead](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-05.html)

# Is "Muphry's law" misspelled on purpose?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** The misspelling is deliberate. John Bangsund, of the Society of Editors (Victoria) in Australia, coined Muphry's law in the society's March 1992 newsletter as "the editorial application of the better-known Murphy's law."

Tell someone: Muphry's law is misspelled on purpose: John Bangsund coined it in 1992 so the law's name would carry its own error.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version takes the name for a slip: someone misspelled Murphy's law and the error stuck.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Society of Editors (Victoria), "Vale John Bangsund" tribute](https://www.iped-editors.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/John-Bangsund-Tribute.pdf)
- [Conversable Economist quoting the 1992 column](https://conversableeconomist.com/2024/07/19/muphrys-law-of-editing-and-proofreading/)
- [HuffPost UK on the Sun's apology](https://huffingtonpost.co.uk/amp/entry/daily-mail-typo_n_5797616)
- [Press Gazette, 10 November 2009](https://pressgazette.co.uk/?p=44585)
- ["Muphry's law," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muphry%27s_law)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Bangsund, "Muphry's Law," Society of Editors (Victoria) Newsletter (1992), reprinted by the Institute of Professional Editors. "Muphry's law," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/muphrys-law/).

# Is the Baader–Meinhof phenomenon named after a militant group?

> Is the Baader–Meinhof phenomenon named after a militant group? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/is-the-baader-meinhof-phenomenon-named-after-a-militant-group.html

Story No. 49 · [Round 5: Names that mislead](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-05.html)

# Is the Baader–Meinhof phenomenon named after a militant group?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** The nickname comes from the West German militant group. It traces to a 1994 reader submission to the *St. Paul Pioneer Press* from a writer who had heard the group's name twice in quick succession.

Tell someone: The Baader–Meinhof phenomenon is named after the West German militant group, by a 1994 newspaper reader who heard its name twice in quick succession.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular assumption is understandable. Two surnames joined by a dash have the look of a scientific eponym, and it is easy to suppose that two researchers stand behind the effect.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Zimmer, "'Frequency illusion' in the OED," Language Log](https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=42180)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: "Frequency illusion," Wikipedia. Zimmer, "'Frequency illusion' in the OED," Language Log. "What's the Baader-Meinhof Phenomenon?," HowStuffWorks. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/baader-meinhof-phenomenon/).

# Is the famous inverted-U stress curve in Yerkes and Dodson's paper?

> Is the famous inverted-U stress curve in Yerkes and Dodson's paper? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/is-the-famous-inverted-u-stress-curve-in-yerkes-and-dodsons-paper.html

Story No. 33 · [Round 4: Charts and numbers](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-04.html)

# Is the famous inverted-U stress curve in Yerkes and Dodson's paper?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The smooth inverted-U curve of stress against performance is not a plot of Yerkes and Dodson's results. Their 1908 paper was a study of mice learning under electric shocks of different strengths.

Tell someone: Yerkes and Dodson's 1908 paper measured no stress and no humans, only how fast forty mice learned under shocks of different strengths.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is a single bell-shaped curve. Performance rises with arousal or stress to a sweet spot, then falls, and the curve is credited to a 1908 study.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Yerkes & Dodson 1908, Classics in the History of Psychology](https://psychclassics.yorku.ca/Yerkes/Law/)
- ["Yerkes-Dodson: Lore, not Law"](https://learningscientists.org/blog/2024/2/29-1)
- ["Yerkes–Dodson law," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yerkes%E2%80%93Dodson_law)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Yerkes & Dodson, "The Relation of Strength of Stimulus to Rapidity of Habit-Formation," *Journal of Comparative Neurology and Psychology* 18 (1908). "Yerkes–Dodson law," Wikipedia. "Yerkes-Dodson: Lore, not Law," The Learning Scientists (2024). The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/yerkes-dodson-law/).

# Is the "invisible hand" the heart of Adam Smith's economics?

> Is the "invisible hand" the heart of Adam Smith's economics? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/is-the-invisible-hand-the-heart-of-adam-smiths-economics.html

Story No. 62 · [Round 7: Words and phrases](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-07.html)

# Is the "invisible hand" the heart of Adam Smith's economics?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Adam Smith used the exact phrase "invisible hand" only three times in his works, and just once in *The Wealth of Nations*. It was not the center of his economics, and he supported many roles for government.

Tell someone: Adam Smith used "invisible hand" just once in *The Wealth of Nations*, and he backed public works, courts and education.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version makes the invisible hand Smith's master idea. The free market, left alone, turns private gain into public good, and Smith built his economics on that principle.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [*The Wealth of Nations*, Project Gutenberg](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/3300/pg3300.txt)
- [Minowitz, EJW](https://econjwatch.org/articles/adam-smith-s-invisible-hands)
- ["Invisible hand," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invisible_hand)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Smith, *The Wealth of Nations* (1776), Book IV, Chapter 2. Minowitz, "Adam Smith's Invisible Hands," *Econ Journal Watch* (2004). "Invisible hand," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/the-invisible-hand/).

# Is the "Mount Stupid" curve from the Dunning–Kruger paper?

> Is the "Mount Stupid" curve from the Dunning–Kruger paper? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/is-the-mount-stupid-curve-from-the-dunning-kruger-paper.html

Story No. 31 · [Round 4: Charts and numbers](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-04.html)

# Is the "Mount Stupid" curve from the Dunning–Kruger paper?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The "Mount Stupid" curve is not in Kruger and Dunning's 1999 paper. The record describes it as a later internet embellishment.

Tell someone: The "Mount Stupid" curve appears nowhere in Kruger and Dunning's 1999 paper, which compared people's estimated rank with their actual test rank.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is a picture. Confidence is plotted against experience. It shoots up to a peak labeled Mount Stupid after a little learning, falls as the size of the subject comes into view, and climbs slowly again with real expertise. The chart is usually captioned as the Dunning–Kruger effect.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Kruger & Dunning 1999, APA archived copy](https://holub.com/goodies/incompetence.pdf)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Kruger & Dunning, "Unskilled and Unaware of It," *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* 77(6) (1999). "Dunning–Kruger effect," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/dunning-kruger-effect/).

# Is the uncertainty principle just about measuring disturbing things?

> Is the uncertainty principle just about measuring disturbing things? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/is-the-uncertainty-principle-just-about-measuring-disturbing-things.html

Story No. 53 · [Round 6: Physics in the kitchen and the sky](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-06.html)

# Is the uncertainty principle just about measuring disturbing things?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The uncertainty principle is not merely the idea that measuring a particle disturbs it. It says a quantum state cannot have sharply defined values of both position and momentum at once, and it holds even for perfect instruments.

Tell someone: The uncertainty principle holds even for perfect instruments, because a quantum state cannot have sharply defined values of both position and momentum at once.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version runs like this: a particle's position and speed cannot both be known, because looking at it knocks it off course.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- ["The Uncertainty Principle," *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-uncertainty/)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Heisenberg, *Zeitschrift für Physik* 43 (1927). "The Uncertainty Principle," *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*. "Uncertainty principle," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/heisenbergs-uncertainty-principle/).

# On most trials, did Asch's subjects go along with the wrong answer?

> On most trials, did Asch's subjects go along with the wrong answer? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/on-most-trials-did-aschs-subjects-go-along-with-the-wrong-answer.html

Story No. 26 · [Round 3: Famous experiments, retold](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-03.html)

# On most trials, did Asch's subjects go along with the wrong answer?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** On most trials, Asch's subjects did not go along. They gave the group's wrong answer on about a third of critical trials and stayed independent on about two-thirds.

Tell someone: Asch's subjects held to what they saw on about two-thirds of critical trials, and one dissenting ally sharply cut conformity.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version holds that people will deny the evidence of their own eyes when a group tells them to. In the retelling, the subjects in Solomon Asch's line experiments usually caved.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- ["Asch conformity experiments," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asch_conformity_experiments)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Asch, "Effects of group pressure upon the modification and distortion of judgments," in *Groups, Leadership and Men* (1951); "Studies of independence and conformity," *Psychological Monographs* (1956). "Asch conformity experiments," Wikipedia. "Asch conformity experiments," Simply Psychology. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/the-asch-conformity-experiments/).

# Round 1: Famous scenes

> Round 1 of True or Folklore?, famous scenes: The stories everyone has heard. A warm-up. Play free online, then see each verdict and its source.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/round-01.html

True or Folklore? · Round 1 of 10

# Round 1: Famous scenes

The stories everyone has heard. A warm-up. Make your call on each story, then tap to see the verdict.

Your score

–

Make a call to start

Playing at a table?

Read each question aloud. Everyone writes TRUE, FOLKLORE or DISPUTED before anyone taps. One point for each right call; DISPUTED only scores if the call was DISPUTED. The book has a two-team scoresheet for this.

Print this round Questions first, then an answer key on its own page.

![Cartoon for the question: Did Archimedes shout "Eureka!" in the bath?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/001.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 1

### [Did Archimedes shout "Eureka!" in the bath?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-archimedes-shout-eureka-in-the-bath.html)

**Folklore.** Archimedes stated the law of buoyancy around 250 BC, in his treatise *On Floating Bodies*. The bath, the crown and the cry of "Eureka!" are almost certainly a later embellishment.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-archimedes-shout-eureka-in-the-bath.html)

![Cartoon for the question: Did an apple fall on Newton's head?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/002.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 2

### [Did an apple fall on Newton's head?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-an-apple-fall-on-newtons-head.html)

**Folklore.** There is an apple in Newton's own account of his thinking about gravity. It does not hit him on the head. That detail is a later embellishment.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-an-apple-fall-on-newtons-head.html)

![Cartoon for the question: Did Newton himself tell the apple story?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/003.png)

TRUE

Round 1 · No. 3

### [Did Newton himself tell the apple story?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-newton-himself-tell-the-apple-story.html)

**True.** The apple story is not a fable invented by Newton's admirers. According to *Encyclopaedia Britannica*, it traces back to Newton's own later recollection. Only the apple hitting his head was added afterward.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-newton-himself-tell-the-apple-story.html)

![Cartoon for the question: Did Galileo drop balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/004.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 4

### [Did Galileo drop balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-galileo-drop-balls-from-the-leaning-tower-of-pisa.html)

**Folklore.** The tower drop is likely a legend. It is not in Galileo's own writings. His documented work on falling bodies used balls rolling down ramps, with notes from around 1603 to 1604 and results published in 1638.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-galileo-drop-balls-from-the-leaning-tower-of-pisa.html)

![Cartoon for the question: Did Pythagoras discover the Pythagorean theorem?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/005.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 5

### [Did Pythagoras discover the Pythagorean theorem?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-pythagoras-discover-the-pythagorean-theorem.html)

**Folklore.** The relation that carries Pythagoras's name was known and used long before him. A Babylonian tablet from around 1800 BC lists its number triples, and Pythagoras lived from about 570 to 495 BC.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-pythagoras-discover-the-pythagorean-theorem.html)

![Cartoon for the question: Did Einstein write E = mc² in his 1905 paper?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/006.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 6

### [Did Einstein write E = mc² in his 1905 paper?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-einstein-write-e-mc2-in-his-1905-paper.html)

**Folklore.** Einstein's 1905 paper contains the idea but not the famous formula. It states in a single sentence that a body which gives off energy as radiation loses mass in proportion.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-einstein-write-e-mc2-in-his-1905-paper.html)

![Cartoon for the question: Did Einstein win his Nobel Prize for something other than relativity?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/007.png)

TRUE

Round 1 · No. 7

### [Did Einstein win his Nobel Prize for something other than relativity?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-einstein-win-his-nobel-prize-for-something-other-than-relativity.html)

**True.** Einstein's Nobel Prize, the physics prize designated for 1921, was for his work on the photoelectric effect. NobelPrize.org gives the citation as "for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect." Relativity is not what the prize named.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-einstein-win-his-nobel-prize-for-something-other-than-relativity.html)

![Cartoon for the question: Did Gordon Moore say chips double every 18 months?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/008.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 8

### [Did Gordon Moore say chips double every 18 months?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-gordon-moore-say-chips-double-every-18-months.html)

**Folklore.** Gordon Moore never gave 18 months. His 1965 article predicted that the number of components on a chip would double roughly every year, and in 1975 he revised that to every two years.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-gordon-moore-say-chips-double-every-18-months.html)

![Cartoon for the question: Did Churchill promise "blood, sweat and tears"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/009.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 9

### [Did Churchill promise "blood, sweat and tears"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-churchill-promise-blood-sweat-and-tears.html)

**Folklore.** In May 1940 Churchill offered "blood, toil, tears and sweat." That is four items, not three, and "toil" is the word that dropped out.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-churchill-promise-blood-sweat-and-tears.html)

![Cartoon for the question: Did Edward Murphy say "Anything that can go wrong will go wrong"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/010.png)

DISPUTED

Round 1 · No. 10

### [Did Edward Murphy say "Anything that can go wrong will go wrong"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-edward-murphy-say-anything-that-can-go-wrong-will-go-wrong.html)

**Disputed.** A maxim like it came out of an Air Force rocket-sled project around 1949, and Murphy's name stuck to it. Who first said it, and in what words, is not settled. The earliest firm printing under Murphy's name, from 1952, credits an unnamed physicist.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-edward-murphy-say-anything-that-can-go-wrong-will-go-wrong.html)

## Answer key

1. Did Archimedes shout "Eureka!" in the bath? **FOLKLORE**
2. Did an apple fall on Newton's head? **FOLKLORE**
3. Did Newton himself tell the apple story? **TRUE**
4. Did Galileo drop balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa? **FOLKLORE**
5. Did Pythagoras discover the Pythagorean theorem? **FOLKLORE**
6. Did Einstein write E = mc² in his 1905 paper? **FOLKLORE**
7. Did Einstein win his Nobel Prize for something other than relativity? **TRUE**
8. Did Gordon Moore say chips double every 18 months? **FOLKLORE**
9. Did Churchill promise "blood, sweat and tears"? **FOLKLORE**
10. Did Edward Murphy say "Anything that can go wrong will go wrong"? **DISPUTED**

# Round 2: Who really said it?

> Round 2 of True or Folklore?: Lines pinned on the wrong person, or on nobody in particular. Play free, then see each verdict and its source.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/round-02.html

True or Folklore? · Round 2 of 10

# Round 2: Who really said it?

Lines pinned on the wrong person, or on nobody in particular. Make your call on each story, then tap to see the verdict.

Your score

–

Make a call to start

Playing at a table?

Read each question aloud. Everyone writes TRUE, FOLKLORE or DISPUTED before anyone taps. One point for each right call; DISPUTED only scores if the call was DISPUTED. The book has a two-team scoresheet for this.

Print this round Questions first, then an answer key on its own page.

Round 2 · No. 11

### [Did William of Ockham write "Entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-william-of-ockham-write-entities-should-not-be-multiplied-beyond-necessity.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The famous Latin sentence is nowhere in Ockham's surviving works. Its earliest close version was written by John Punch in 1639, nearly three centuries after Ockham died. Ockham argued for the same principle, in other words.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-william-of-ockham-write-entities-should-not-be-multiplied-beyond-necessity.html)

Round 2 · No. 12

### [Did Hebb say "neurons that fire together wire together"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-hebb-say-neurons-that-fire-together-wire-together.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Donald Hebb set out the rule in 1949. The slogan is not his. It came in 1992, usually credited to Carla Shatz as a mnemonic, and crediting it to Hebb is, in the record's words, the most common error about the rule.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-hebb-say-neurons-that-fire-together-wire-together.html)

Round 2 · No. 13

### [Did Mark Twain say "If all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-mark-twain-say-if-all-you-have-is-a-hammer-everything-looks-like-a-nail.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** There is no evidence that Mark Twain said it. The idea was named by the philosopher Abraham Kaplan in 1964, after a talk in 1962. Its best-known hammer-and-nail form is Abraham Maslow's, from 1966.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-mark-twain-say-if-all-you-have-is-a-hammer-everything-looks-like-a-nail.html)

Round 2 · No. 14

### [Did Goodhart say "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-goodhart-say-when-a-measure-becomes-a-target-it-ceases-to-be-a-good-measure.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The famous sentence is Marilyn Strathern's, from 1997. Charles Goodhart's original point, in 1975, was narrower and about monetary policy.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-goodhart-say-when-a-measure-becomes-a-target-it-ceases-to-be-a-good-measure.html)

Round 2 · No. 15

### [Did a real Robert Hanlon coin Hanlon's razor?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-a-real-robert-hanlon-coin-hanlons-razor.html)

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** The razor is generally credited to a Robert J. Hanlon, but the evidence for him is second-hand. Its first appearance in print, in a 1980 book, gives the name "Hanlon" with no indication of who he was.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-a-real-robert-hanlon-coin-hanlons-razor.html)

Round 2 · No. 16

### [Did Napoleon say "Never attribute to malice what can be explained by stupidity"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-napoleon-say-never-attribute-to-malice-what-can-be-explained-by-stupidity.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The line is not Napoleon's. Quote Investigator, the source the record cites for its dated history of the saying, debunks the Napoleon attribution. The earliest known printing of the razor is from 1980.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-napoleon-say-never-attribute-to-malice-what-can-be-explained-by-stupidity.html)

Round 2 · No. 17

### [Did Godwin say whoever mentions Hitler first loses?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-godwin-say-whoever-mentions-hitler-first-loses.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Mike Godwin's 1990 law says only that a long online argument is likely to produce a comparison to Hitler or the Nazis. The rule that whoever makes the comparison loses was added later by the Usenet community, not by Godwin.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-godwin-say-whoever-mentions-hitler-first-loses.html)

Round 2 · No. 18

### [Did Sturgeon say "Ninety percent of everything is crap"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-sturgeon-say-ninety-percent-of-everything-is-crap.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Theodore Sturgeon's printed word was "crud," not "crap." His *Venture Science Fiction* column first printed it in September 1957. In March 1958 the column gave it as "Ninety percent of everything is crud." He also called it his Revelation, not his law.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-sturgeon-say-ninety-percent-of-everything-is-crap.html)

Round 2 · No. 19

### [Did Twain or Einstein say "A man with one watch knows what time it is"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-twain-or-einstein-say-a-man-with-one-watch-knows-what-time-it-is.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Neither did. The saying first appears without a name in the *San Diego Union* in 1930. The attributions to Mark Twain and Albert Einstein are unsupported, and no documented Segal wrote it either.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-twain-or-einstein-say-a-man-with-one-watch-knows-what-time-it-is.html)

Round 2 · No. 20

### [Did Henry Kissinger say academic politics are vicious because the stakes are so small?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-henry-kissinger-say-academic-politics-are-vicious-because-the-stakes-are-so-small.html)

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** The line has been credited to Henry Kissinger, but he is one of several claimants, and none has a clean title. The record calls the attribution famously tangled. Its usual namesake is the Columbia political scientist Wallace Sayre, and Quote Investigator traces the idea back to Samuel Johnson in 1765.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-henry-kissinger-say-academic-politics-are-vicious-because-the-stakes-are-so-small.html)

## Answer key

1. Did William of Ockham write "Entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity"? **FOLKLORE**
2. Did Hebb say "neurons that fire together wire together"? **FOLKLORE**
3. Did Mark Twain say "If all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail"? **FOLKLORE**
4. Did Goodhart say "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure"? **FOLKLORE**
5. Did a real Robert Hanlon coin Hanlon's razor? **DISPUTED**
6. Did Napoleon say "Never attribute to malice what can be explained by stupidity"? **FOLKLORE**
7. Did Godwin say whoever mentions Hitler first loses? **FOLKLORE**
8. Did Sturgeon say "Ninety percent of everything is crap"? **FOLKLORE**
9. Did Twain or Einstein say "A man with one watch knows what time it is"? **FOLKLORE**
10. Did Henry Kissinger say academic politics are vicious because the stakes are so small? **DISPUTED**

# Round 3: Famous experiments, retold

> Round 3 of True or Folklore?, famous experiments, retold: What the textbook version leaves out. Play free online, then see each verdict and its source.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/round-03.html

True or Folklore? · Round 3 of 10

# Round 3: Famous experiments, retold

What the textbook version leaves out. Make your call on each story, then tap to see the verdict.

Your score

–

Make a call to start

Playing at a table?

Read each question aloud. Everyone writes TRUE, FOLKLORE or DISPUTED before anyone taps. One point for each right call; DISPUTED only scores if the call was DISPUTED. The book has a two-team scoresheet for this.

Print this round Questions first, then an answer key on its own page.

Round 3 · No. 21

### [Did 38 witnesses watch Kitty Genovese die and do nothing?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-38-witnesses-watch-kitty-genovese-die-and-do-nothing.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The record finds no basis for the story that 38 witnesses watched Kitty Genovese die and did nothing. At least one witness shouted at her attacker.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-38-witnesses-watch-kitty-genovese-die-and-do-nothing.html)

Round 3 · No. 22

### [Did the Stanford prison guards turn cruel on their own?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-the-stanford-prison-guards-turn-cruel-on-their-own.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The guards did not become cruel on their own. Archival recordings and later scholarship show that the experimenters, including the warden, instructed and pressured them to be tough.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-the-stanford-prison-guards-turn-cruel-on-their-own.html)

Round 3 · No. 23

### [Did Hawthorne factory output rise whatever the lighting?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-hawthorne-factory-output-rise-whatever-the-lighting.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The original Hawthorne lighting data do not show output rising whatever the lighting. When Steven Levitt and John List reanalyzed them, they called the famous patterns "entirely fictional".

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-hawthorne-factory-output-rise-whatever-the-lighting.html)

Round 3 · No. 24

### [Did 65% of Milgram's volunteers give the maximum shock?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-65-of-milgrams-volunteers-give-the-maximum-shock.html)

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** About 65 percent of participants went to the maximum 450 volts in one baseline condition. Across the more than twenty conditions Milgram ran, obedience varied widely, and archival research has questioned how many participants believed the shocks were real.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-65-of-milgrams-volunteers-give-the-maximum-shock.html)

Round 3 · No. 25

### [Did Milgram prove we are all six handshakes apart?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-milgram-prove-we-are-all-six-handshakes-apart.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Milgram did not prove that everyone is six handshakes apart. Most of the chains in his 1967 experiment never reached their target, and the "six" is a median over the minority that did.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-milgram-prove-we-are-all-six-handshakes-apart.html)

Round 3 · No. 26

### [On most trials, did Asch's subjects go along with the wrong answer?](https://conyso.com/publishing/on-most-trials-did-aschs-subjects-go-along-with-the-wrong-answer.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** On most trials, Asch's subjects did not go along. They gave the group's wrong answer on about a third of critical trials and stayed independent on about two-thirds.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/on-most-trials-did-aschs-subjects-go-along-with-the-wrong-answer.html)

Round 3 · No. 27

### [Does waiting for a second marshmallow predict success in life?](https://conyso.com/publishing/does-waiting-for-a-second-marshmallow-predict-success-in-life.html)

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** Early follow-ups linked a preschooler's ability to wait with later achievement. A larger 2018 replication found the link much weaker and largely explained by family background.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/does-waiting-for-a-second-marshmallow-predict-success-in-life.html)

Round 3 · No. 28

### [Did the Robbers Cave study have a failed first attempt?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-the-robbers-cave-study-have-a-failed-first-attempt.html)

TRUE

**True.** Before the famous 1954 Robbers Cave study, Muzafer Sherif ran a pilot in 1953 that failed. The boys resisted the hostility the researchers tried to induce, and suspected the staff.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-the-robbers-cave-study-have-a-failed-first-attempt.html)

Round 3 · No. 29

### [Was the forgetting curve based on just one person?](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-the-forgetting-curve-based-on-just-one-person.html)

TRUE

**True.** The forgetting curve rests on one subject: Hermann Ebbinghaus, who tested himself. Its best-known modern replication, in 2015, also used essentially one subject.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-the-forgetting-curve-based-on-just-one-person.html)

Round 3 · No. 30

### [Do we know what became of Little Albert?](https://conyso.com/publishing/do-we-know-what-became-of-little-albert.html)

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** No one has settled who Little Albert was or what became of him. Rival candidates have been proposed, and the record says there is no settled answer.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/do-we-know-what-became-of-little-albert.html)

## Answer key

1. Did 38 witnesses watch Kitty Genovese die and do nothing? **FOLKLORE**
2. Did the Stanford prison guards turn cruel on their own? **FOLKLORE**
3. Did Hawthorne factory output rise whatever the lighting? **FOLKLORE**
4. Did 65% of Milgram's volunteers give the maximum shock? **DISPUTED**
5. Did Milgram prove we are all six handshakes apart? **FOLKLORE**
6. On most trials, did Asch's subjects go along with the wrong answer? **FOLKLORE**
7. Does waiting for a second marshmallow predict success in life? **DISPUTED**
8. Did the Robbers Cave study have a failed first attempt? **TRUE**
9. Was the forgetting curve based on just one person? **TRUE**
10. Do we know what became of Little Albert? **DISPUTED**

10 stories in this round online.

True or Folklore? · Round 4 of 10

# Round 4: Charts and numbers

Famous pictures and figures, checked against the original. Make your call on each story, then tap to see the verdict.

Make a call to start

Playing at a table?

Read each question aloud. Everyone writes TRUE, FOLKLORE or DISPUTED before anyone taps. One point for each right call; DISPUTED only scores if the call was DISPUTED. The book has a two-team scoresheet for this.

Print this round Questions first, then an answer key on its own page.

Round 4 · No. 31

### [Is the "Mount Stupid" curve from the Dunning–Kruger paper?](https://conyso.com/publishing/is-the-mount-stupid-curve-from-the-dunning-kruger-paper.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The "Mount Stupid" curve is not in Kruger and Dunning's 1999 paper. The record describes it as a later internet embellishment.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/is-the-mount-stupid-curve-from-the-dunning-kruger-paper.html)

Round 4 · No. 32

### [Do the least skilled people really overrate themselves the most?](https://conyso.com/publishing/do-the-least-skilled-people-really-overrate-themselves-the-most.html)

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** In 1999 Kruger and Dunning found that the lowest scorers on several tests overestimated their rank. Since 2016 several researchers have argued that much of that pattern is a statistical artifact, and a 2026 reanalysis reports that it inverts.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/do-the-least-skilled-people-really-overrate-themselves-the-most.html)

Round 4 · No. 33

### [Is the famous inverted-U stress curve in Yerkes and Dodson's paper?](https://conyso.com/publishing/is-the-famous-inverted-u-stress-curve-in-yerkes-and-dodsons-paper.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The smooth inverted-U curve of stress against performance is not a plot of Yerkes and Dodson's results. Their 1908 paper was a study of mice learning under electric shocks of different strengths.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/is-the-famous-inverted-u-stress-curve-in-yerkes-and-dodsons-paper.html)

Round 4 · No. 34

### [Did Maslow draw the pyramid of needs?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-maslow-draw-the-pyramid-of-needs.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Maslow did not draw the pyramid. The famous diagram was created by later authors, not by Maslow himself.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-maslow-draw-the-pyramid-of-needs.html)

Round 4 · No. 35

### [Did Abraham Wald draw the famous bullet-hole plane?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-abraham-wald-draw-the-famous-bullet-hole-plane.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Abraham Wald did not draw the bomber covered in red dots. The record describes that image as a designer's later recreation, a teaching device from decades after the war.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-abraham-wald-draw-the-famous-bullet-hole-plane.html)

Round 4 · No. 36

### [Did Wald really tell the military to armor where returning planes weren't hit?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-wald-really-tell-the-military-to-armor-where-returning-planes-werent-hit.html)

TRUE

**True.** The reasoning in the famous story is Wald's. In his 1943 memoranda he estimated aircraft vulnerability from the damage on returning planes, while accounting for the planes that did not return.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-wald-really-tell-the-military-to-armor-where-returning-planes-werent-hit.html)

Round 4 · No. 38

### [Was Benford's law first spotted in worn logarithm tables?](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-benfords-law-first-spotted-in-worn-logarithm-tables.html)

TRUE

**True.** The astronomer Simon Newcomb first noticed the leading-digit law in 1881, from the observation that the early pages of logarithm tables, those for numbers starting with 1, were the most worn. Frank Benford rediscovered it in 1938.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-benfords-law-first-spotted-in-worn-logarithm-tables.html)

Round 4 · No. 40

### [Did Marilyn vos Savant's correct Monty Hall answer draw a storm of objections?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-marilyn-vos-savants-correct-monty-hall-answer-draw-a-storm-of-objections.html)

TRUE

**True.** When Marilyn vos Savant gave the correct answer to the Monty Hall problem in 1990, some ten thousand readers wrote in, close to a thousand of them with doctorates, insisting she was wrong.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-marilyn-vos-savants-correct-monty-hall-answer-draw-a-storm-of-objections.html)

## Answer key

1. Is the "Mount Stupid" curve from the Dunning–Kruger paper? **FOLKLORE**
2. Do the least skilled people really overrate themselves the most? **DISPUTED**
3. Is the famous inverted-U stress curve in Yerkes and Dodson's paper? **FOLKLORE**
4. Did Maslow draw the pyramid of needs? **FOLKLORE**
5. Did Abraham Wald draw the famous bullet-hole plane? **FOLKLORE**
6. Did Wald really tell the military to armor where returning planes weren't hit? **TRUE**
7. Was Benford's law first spotted in worn logarithm tables? **TRUE**
8. Did Marilyn vos Savant's correct Monty Hall answer draw a storm of objections? **TRUE**

# Round 5: Names that mislead

> Round 5 of True or Folklore?: Laws named after people who did not find them, and odder naming stories. Play free, then see each verdict and its source.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/round-05.html

True or Folklore? · Round 5 of 10

# Round 5: Names that mislead

Laws named after people who did not find them, and odder naming stories. Make your call on each story, then tap to see the verdict.

Your score

–

Make a call to start

Playing at a table?

Read each question aloud. Everyone writes TRUE, FOLKLORE or DISPUTED before anyone taps. One point for each right call; DISPUTED only scores if the call was DISPUTED. The book has a two-team scoresheet for this.

Print this round Questions first, then an answer key on its own page.

Round 5 · No. 41

### [Did Stigler credit Stigler's law to someone else?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-stigler-credit-stiglers-law-to-someone-else.html)

TRUE

**True.** In the 1980 paper that named the law after himself, the statistician Stephen Stigler credited its discovery to the sociologist Robert K. Merton. The law says no scientific discovery is named after its original discoverer, so it was built to obey itself.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-stigler-credit-stiglers-law-to-someone-else.html)

Round 5 · No. 42

### [Did Maxwell write the four Maxwell's equations?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-maxwell-write-the-four-maxwells-equations.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** James Clerk Maxwell built the theory, but the four compact equations that carry his name are Oliver Heaviside's reformulation of 1884. Maxwell's own 1865 paper contained twenty equations.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-maxwell-write-the-four-maxwells-equations.html)

Round 5 · No. 44

### [Did Thomas Gresham formulate Gresham's law?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-thomas-gresham-formulate-greshams-law.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Thomas Gresham did not formulate Gresham's law. Henry Dunning Macleod named it after him in 1858, and the principle had been stated long before: by Oresme, by Copernicus around 1519, and in Aristophanes' play *The Frogs* around 405 BC.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-thomas-gresham-formulate-greshams-law.html)

Round 5 · No. 45

### [Was Hubble the first to find Hubble's law?](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-hubble-the-first-to-find-hubbles-law.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Georges Lemaître derived the relation between a galaxy's distance and its speed of recession, and estimated its constant, in 1927. Edwin Hubble's paper came two years later, in 1929. In 2018 the International Astronomical Union recommended renaming the law the Hubble–Lemaître law.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-hubble-the-first-to-find-hubbles-law.html)

Round 5 · No. 47

### [Does Laffer himself say the Laffer curve wasn't his idea?](https://conyso.com/publishing/does-laffer-himself-say-the-laffer-curve-wasnt-his-idea.html)

TRUE

**True.** Arthur Laffer has disclaimed originality for the curve that bears his name. He credits earlier sources, including Ibn Khaldun in the fourteenth century and John Maynard Keynes.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/does-laffer-himself-say-the-laffer-curve-wasnt-his-idea.html)

Round 5 · No. 48

### [Was the Overton window named only after Overton's death?](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-the-overton-window-named-only-after-overtons-death.html)

TRUE

**True.** Joseph P. Overton developed the idea in the mid-1990s, but it was his colleague Joseph Lehman who named and elaborated it, after Overton died in a 2003 ultralight-aircraft crash.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-the-overton-window-named-only-after-overtons-death.html)

Round 5 · No. 49

### [Is the Baader–Meinhof phenomenon named after a militant group?](https://conyso.com/publishing/is-the-baader-meinhof-phenomenon-named-after-a-militant-group.html)

TRUE

**True.** The nickname comes from the West German militant group. It traces to a 1994 reader submission to the *St. Paul Pioneer Press* from a writer who had heard the group's name twice in quick succession.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/is-the-baader-meinhof-phenomenon-named-after-a-militant-group.html)

Round 5 · No. 50

### [Is "Muphry's law" misspelled on purpose?](https://conyso.com/publishing/is-muphrys-law-misspelled-on-purpose.html)

TRUE

**True.** The misspelling is deliberate. John Bangsund, of the Society of Editors (Victoria) in Australia, coined Muphry's law in the society's March 1992 newsletter as "the editorial application of the better-known Murphy's law."

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/is-muphrys-law-misspelled-on-purpose.html)

## Answer key

1. Did Stigler credit Stigler's law to someone else? **TRUE**
2. Did Maxwell write the four Maxwell's equations? **FOLKLORE**
3. Did Thomas Gresham formulate Gresham's law? **FOLKLORE**
4. Was Hubble the first to find Hubble's law? **FOLKLORE**
5. Does Laffer himself say the Laffer curve wasn't his idea? **TRUE**
6. Was the Overton window named only after Overton's death? **TRUE**
7. Is the Baader–Meinhof phenomenon named after a militant group? **TRUE**
8. Is "Muphry's law" misspelled on purpose? **TRUE**

8 stories in this round online. 2 more stories are in the book and go up here once each verdict is final.

[Round 6: Physics in the kitchen and the sky →](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-06.html) [All rounds](https://conyso.com/publishing/true-or-folklore.html#rounds)

# Round 6: Physics in the kitchen and the sky

> Round 6 of True or Folklore?, physics in the kitchen and the sky: Everyday science myths. Play free online, then see each verdict and its source.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/round-06.html

True or Folklore? · Round 6 of 10

# Round 6: Physics in the kitchen and the sky

Everyday science myths. Make your call on each story, then tap to see the verdict.

Your score

–

Make a call to start

Playing at a table?

Read each question aloud. Everyone writes TRUE, FOLKLORE or DISPUTED before anyone taps. One point for each right call; DISPUTED only scores if the call was DISPUTED. The book has a two-team scoresheet for this.

Print this round Questions first, then an answer key on its own page.

Round 6 · No. 52

### [Does the Coriolis effect decide which way a sink drains?](https://conyso.com/publishing/does-the-coriolis-effect-decide-which-way-a-sink-drains.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** At the scale of a sink, bath or toilet, the Coriolis effect is thousands of times too weak to set the direction of draining. Water drains both ways within the same hemisphere.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/does-the-coriolis-effect-decide-which-way-a-sink-drains.html)

Round 6 · No. 53

### [Is the uncertainty principle just about measuring disturbing things?](https://conyso.com/publishing/is-the-uncertainty-principle-just-about-measuring-disturbing-things.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The uncertainty principle is not merely the idea that measuring a particle disturbs it. It says a quantum state cannot have sharply defined values of both position and momentum at once, and it holds even for perfect instruments.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/is-the-uncertainty-principle-just-about-measuring-disturbing-things.html)

Round 6 · No. 54

### [Was Schrödinger's cat meant to make a quantum idea look absurd?](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-schrodingers-cat-meant-to-make-a-quantum-idea-look-absurd.html)

TRUE

**True.** Erwin Schrödinger devised the cat in 1935 as an objection to the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics. His aim was to show the absurdity of extending quantum superposition to a large object, not to claim that a cat can be alive and dead at once.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-schrodingers-cat-meant-to-make-a-quantum-idea-look-absurd.html)

Round 6 · No. 55

### [Did vortex shedding bring down the Tacoma Narrows Bridge?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-vortex-shedding-bring-down-the-tacoma-narrows-bridge.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The 1940 collapse of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge is more accurately explained by aeroelastic flutter, a distinct, self-excited mechanism. The record says the case should not be presented as simple vortex-street resonance.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-vortex-shedding-bring-down-the-tacoma-narrows-bridge.html)

Round 6 · No. 56

### [Does air over a wing speed up to meet the air underneath?](https://conyso.com/publishing/does-air-over-a-wing-speed-up-to-meet-the-air-underneath.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Air does move faster over a wing's upper surface, and the pressure there is lower. But the popular reason, that the air must hurry to rejoin the air beneath, is a misconception that NASA debunks.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/does-air-over-a-wing-speed-up-to-meet-the-air-underneath.html)

Round 6 · No. 57

### [Does hot water freeze faster than cold?](https://conyso.com/publishing/does-hot-water-freeze-faster-than-cold.html)

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** Whether hot water can freeze faster than cold is unresolved. Erasto Mpemba and Denis Osborne published the claim in 1969, a careful 2016 study by Burridge and Linden found no evidence for a meaningful effect, and the record says the dispute remains open.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/does-hot-water-freeze-faster-than-cold.html)

Round 6 · No. 58

### [Does a broken bone heal back stronger?](https://conyso.com/publishing/does-a-broken-bone-heal-back-stronger.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** There is no evidence, contrary to popular belief, that a healed fracture becomes stronger than the original unbroken bone. The claim is an overstatement of Wolff's law, which describes how healthy bone adapts to the loads placed on it.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/does-a-broken-bone-heal-back-stronger.html)

Round 6 · No. 59

### [Did Thomas Young shine light through two slits?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-thomas-young-shine-light-through-two-slits.html)

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** Thomas Young showed that light interferes, in his Bakerian Lectures around 1801 and 1803. Whether he performed a literal two-slit experiment is disputed: his demonstrations used sunlight, pinholes and narrow cards.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-thomas-young-shine-light-through-two-slits.html)

Round 6 · No. 60

### [Was the Doppler effect tested with trumpeters on a train?](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-the-doppler-effect-tested-with-trumpeters-on-a-train.html)

TRUE

**True.** C. H. D. Buys Ballot tested the Doppler effect for sound in 1845, using trumpeters on a moving train. Christian Doppler had predicted the effect three years earlier, in an 1842 paper in Prague.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-the-doppler-effect-tested-with-trumpeters-on-a-train.html)

## Answer key

1. Does the Coriolis effect decide which way a sink drains? **FOLKLORE**
2. Is the uncertainty principle just about measuring disturbing things? **FOLKLORE**
3. Was Schrödinger's cat meant to make a quantum idea look absurd? **TRUE**
4. Did vortex shedding bring down the Tacoma Narrows Bridge? **FOLKLORE**
5. Does air over a wing speed up to meet the air underneath? **FOLKLORE**
6. Does hot water freeze faster than cold? **DISPUTED**
7. Does a broken bone heal back stronger? **FOLKLORE**
8. Did Thomas Young shine light through two slits? **DISPUTED**
9. Was the Doppler effect tested with trumpeters on a train? **TRUE**

9 stories in this round online. 1 more story is in the book and goes up here once its verdict is final.

# Round 7: Words and phrases

> Round 7 of True or Folklore?, words and phrases: Where the famous expressions really come from. Play free online, then see each verdict and its source.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/round-07.html

True or Folklore? · Round 7 of 10

# Round 7: Words and phrases

Where the famous expressions really come from. Make your call on each story, then tap to see the verdict.

Your score

–

Make a call to start

Playing at a table?

Read each question aloud. Everyone writes TRUE, FOLKLORE or DISPUTED before anyone taps. One point for each right call; DISPUTED only scores if the call was DISPUTED. The book has a two-team scoresheet for this.

Print this round Questions first, then an answer key on its own page.

Round 7 · No. 61

### [Does "red herring" come from training hounds with smoked fish?](https://conyso.com/publishing/does-red-herring-come-from-training-hounds-with-smoked-fish.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The hound-training origin is likely a myth. The figurative sense of "red herring" is real, and it is traceable to the journalist William Cobbett in 1807.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/does-red-herring-come-from-training-hounds-with-smoked-fish.html)

Round 7 · No. 62

### [Is the "invisible hand" the heart of Adam Smith's economics?](https://conyso.com/publishing/is-the-invisible-hand-the-heart-of-adam-smiths-economics.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Adam Smith used the exact phrase "invisible hand" only three times in his works, and just once in *The Wealth of Nations*. It was not the center of his economics, and he supported many roles for government.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/is-the-invisible-hand-the-heart-of-adam-smiths-economics.html)

Round 7 · No. 63

### [Did Say write "supply creates its own demand"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-say-write-supply-creates-its-own-demand.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The phrase "supply creates its own demand" does not appear in Jean-Baptiste Say's own writing. John Maynard Keynes popularized it in 1936, and even Keynes seems to have been quoting a phrase already current.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-say-write-supply-creates-its-own-demand.html)

Round 7 · No. 64

### [Did habeas corpus come from Magna Carta?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-habeas-corpus-come-from-magna-carta.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Habeas corpus did not come from Magna Carta. Its roots predate the charter of 1215. It grew out of English common law over centuries, and the Habeas Corpus Act of 1679 codified it.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-habeas-corpus-come-from-magna-carta.html)

Round 7 · No. 65

### [Did Rousseau coin "the noble savage"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-rousseau-coin-the-noble-savage.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Jean-Jacques Rousseau did not coin "the noble savage." The phrase does not appear in his writings and was pinned on him later.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-rousseau-coin-the-noble-savage.html)

Round 7 · No. 66

### [Did Clausewitz coin "the fog of war"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-clausewitz-coin-the-fog-of-war.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Carl von Clausewitz did not coin "the fog of war." In *On War* (1832) he conveyed the uncertainty of war through images of fog, twilight and moonlight. The crisp phrase is a later paraphrase, prominent partly because a twentieth-century translation chose the word "fog."

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-clausewitz-coin-the-fog-of-war.html)

Round 7 · No. 67

### [Was the acronym "MAD" a critic's jibe?](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-the-acronym-mad-a-critics-jibe.html)

TRUE

**True.** The acronym MAD is attributed to a critic, Donald Brennan of the Hudson Institute, who used it derisively to argue that the nuclear posture it named was irrational. Robert McNamara, under whom the doctrine took shape, promoted "assured destruction," not MAD.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-the-acronym-mad-a-critics-jibe.html)

Round 7 · No. 68

### [Was "moving the goalposts" used in Parliament a century ago?](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-moving-the-goalposts-used-in-parliament-a-century-ago.html)

TRUE

**True.** The earliest documented figurative use of the phrase is in a House of Commons debate on 2 May 1924. The idiom is British, and it was in political speech some sixty years before it came into widespread use in the 1980s.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-moving-the-goalposts-used-in-parliament-a-century-ago.html)

Round 7 · No. 69

### [Did Weber write "iron cage"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-weber-write-iron-cage.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Max Weber did not write "iron cage." The English phrase is Talcott Parsons's 1930 translation of Weber's German *stahlhartes Gehäuse*, which more literally means a shell or casing as hard as steel.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-weber-write-iron-cage.html)

Round 7 · No. 70

### [Did Richard Dawkins coin the word "meme"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-richard-dawkins-coin-the-word-meme.html)

TRUE

**True.** Richard Dawkins coined the word "meme" in his 1976 book *The Selfish Gene*, as the name for a unit of cultural transmission.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-richard-dawkins-coin-the-word-meme.html)

## Answer key

1. Does "red herring" come from training hounds with smoked fish? **FOLKLORE**
2. Is the "invisible hand" the heart of Adam Smith's economics? **FOLKLORE**
3. Did Say write "supply creates its own demand"? **FOLKLORE**
4. Did habeas corpus come from Magna Carta? **FOLKLORE**
5. Did Rousseau coin "the noble savage"? **FOLKLORE**
6. Did Clausewitz coin "the fog of war"? **FOLKLORE**
7. Was the acronym "MAD" a critic's jibe? **TRUE**
8. Was "moving the goalposts" used in Parliament a century ago? **TRUE**
9. Did Weber write "iron cage"? **FOLKLORE**
10. Did Richard Dawkins coin the word "meme"? **TRUE**

10 stories in this round online.

# Round 8: Jokes that became laws

> Round 8 of True or Folklore?: Satire, office humor and asides that hardened into rules. Play free, then see each verdict and its source.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/round-08.html

True or Folklore? · Round 8 of 10

# Round 8: Jokes that became laws

Satire, office humor and asides that hardened into rules. Make your call on each story, then tap to see the verdict.

Your score

–

Make a call to start

Playing at a table?

Read each question aloud. Everyone writes TRUE, FOLKLORE or DISPUTED before anyone taps. One point for each right call; DISPUTED only scores if the call was DISPUTED. The book has a two-team scoresheet for this.

Print this round Questions first, then an answer key on its own page.

Round 8 · No. 71

### [Did Parkinson's law begin as a joke in *The Economist*?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-parkinsons-law-begin-as-a-joke-in-the-economist.html)

TRUE

**True.** Parkinson's law began as satire. The naval historian C. Northcote Parkinson opened a satirical essay in *The Economist* on 19 November 1955 with the "commonplace observation" that made his name: work "expands so as to fill the time available for its completion."

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-parkinsons-law-begin-as-a-joke-in-the-economist.html)

Round 8 · No. 72

### [Was the Peter Principle written as satire?](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-the-peter-principle-written-as-satire.html)

TRUE

**True.** The Peter Principle was pitched as satire. The educator Laurence J. Peter and the playwright Raymond Hull set it out in their 1969 book: "In a hierarchy, every employee tends to rise to his level of incompetence." It landed as serious management theory.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-the-peter-principle-written-as-satire.html)

Round 8 · No. 73

### [Was there a real committee that argued over a bike shed?](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-there-a-real-committee-that-argued-over-a-bike-shed.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** No real meeting lies behind the story. The reactor, the bicycle shed and the refreshment budget are C. Northcote Parkinson's invented example, from his 1957 book *Parkinson's Law, or The Pursuit of Progress*.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-there-a-real-committee-that-argued-over-a-bike-shed.html)

Round 8 · No. 74

### [Did Brooks admit his own law was an oversimplification?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-brooks-admit-his-own-law-was-an-oversimplification.html)

TRUE

**True.** Fred Brooks, who coined Brooks's law in *The Mythical Man-Month* (1975), freely admitted that the law oversimplifies a real tendency: he introduced it with the words "Oversimplifying outrageously."

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-brooks-admit-his-own-law-was-an-oversimplification.html)

Round 8 · No. 75

### [Did Clarke add "Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic" years later?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-clarke-add-any-sufficiently-advanced-technology-is-indistinguishable-from-magic-years-later.html)

TRUE

**True.** Arthur C. Clarke's most famous law came last. He stated his First and Second Laws in 1962 and added the Third, "Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic," to the revised 1973 edition of the same book, having first published it in a 1968 letter to *Science*.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-clarke-add-any-sufficiently-advanced-technology-is-indistinguishable-from-magic-years-later.html)

Round 8 · No. 76

### [Has toast landing butter-side down been studied seriously?](https://conyso.com/publishing/has-toast-landing-butter-side-down-been-studied-seriously.html)

TRUE

**True.** In 1995 the physicist Robert Matthews published "Tumbling toast, Murphy's Law and the fundamental constants" in the *European Journal of Physics*. It won a 1996 Ig Nobel Prize, and it argued that toast does tend to land butter-side down, for mundane physical reasons.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/has-toast-landing-butter-side-down-been-studied-seriously.html)

Round 8 · No. 77

### [Did *Harvard Business Review* reject Conway's law?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-harvard-business-review-reject-conways-law.html)

TRUE

**True.** By Melvin Conway's own account, *Harvard Business Review* rejected his paper on the grounds that he had not proved his thesis. "How Do Committees Invent?" appeared instead in *Datamation* in April 1968.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-harvard-business-review-reject-conways-law.html)

Round 8 · No. 78

### [Did Philip Greenspun write rules one to nine?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-philip-greenspun-write-rules-one-to-nine.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** There are no rules one to nine. The "tenth" in Greenspun's Tenth Rule is itself the joke; Philip Greenspun has said he just wanted a memorable name.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-philip-greenspun-write-rules-one-to-nine.html)

Round 8 · No. 79

### [Did Kelly Johnson coin "Keep it simple, stupid"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-kelly-johnson-coin-keep-it-simple-stupid.html)

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** The phrase is attributed to Kelly Johnson, lead engineer at Lockheed's Skunk Works, but the attribution is not airtight. A 1938 *Minneapolis Star* article used the variant "keep it short and simple," before Johnson's association with the phrase, and the earliest dated record of the acronym itself is a U.S. Navy "Project KISS" in 1960.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-kelly-johnson-coin-keep-it-simple-stupid.html)

Round 8 · No. 80

### [Did Fermi pose the Fermi paradox over lunch?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-fermi-pose-the-fermi-paradox-over-lunch.html)

TRUE

**True.** The question began as a lunchtime remark by the physicist Enrico Fermi at Los Alamos in 1950, with his colleagues Teller, Konopinski and York. Firsthand accounts differ on his exact words, and the paradox's name and rigorous form came later, from others.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-fermi-pose-the-fermi-paradox-over-lunch.html)

## Answer key

1. Did Parkinson's law begin as a joke in *The Economist*? **TRUE**
2. Was the Peter Principle written as satire? **TRUE**
3. Was there a real committee that argued over a bike shed? **FOLKLORE**
4. Did Brooks admit his own law was an oversimplification? **TRUE**
5. Did Clarke add "Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic" years later? **TRUE**
6. Has toast landing butter-side down been studied seriously? **TRUE**
7. Did *Harvard Business Review* reject Conway's law? **TRUE**
8. Did Philip Greenspun write rules one to nine? **FOLKLORE**
9. Did Kelly Johnson coin "Keep it simple, stupid"? **DISPUTED**
10. Did Fermi pose the Fermi paradox over lunch? **TRUE**
