# Round 9: Discovery stories

> Round 9 of True or Folklore?, discovery stories: Who found what, and how the credit was shared out. Play free online, then see each verdict and its source.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/round-09.html

True or Folklore? · Round 9 of 10

# Round 9: Discovery stories

Who found what, and how the credit was shared out. Make your call on each story, then tap to see the verdict.

Your score

–

Make a call to start

Playing at a table?

Read each question aloud. Everyone writes TRUE, FOLKLORE or DISPUTED before anyone taps. One point for each right call; DISPUTED only scores if the call was DISPUTED. The book has a two-team scoresheet for this.

Print this round Questions first, then an answer key on its own page.

Round 9 · No. 81

### [Was Photo 51 taken by Raymond Gosling?](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-photo-51-taken-by-raymond-gosling.html)

TRUE

**True.** Raymond Gosling, a doctoral student, took Photo 51 at King's College London in May 1952, while working under Rosalind Franklin's supervision. The credit belongs to both of them.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-photo-51-taken-by-raymond-gosling.html)

Round 9 · No. 82

### [Did Watson and Crick steal Rosalind Franklin's data?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-watson-and-crick-steal-rosalind-franklins-data.html)

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** The record documents that Maurice Wilkins showed Photo 51 to James Watson without Franklin's knowledge, and that her data shaped the 1953 model. Recent scholarship argues that this was not a simple story of theft.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-watson-and-crick-steal-rosalind-franklins-data.html)

Round 9 · No. 83

### [Did Philippa Foot invent the trolley problem?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-philippa-foot-invent-the-trolley-problem.html)

TRUE

**True.** Philippa Foot introduced the original case in 1967, in a paper called "The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of the Double Effect." She did not name it. Judith Jarvis Thomson called it the trolley problem and added its best-known variants in 1976 and 1985.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-philippa-foot-invent-the-trolley-problem.html)

Round 9 · No. 84

### [Was Wegener the first to notice the continents fit together?](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-wegener-the-first-to-notice-the-continents-fit-together.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Alfred Wegener was not the first. Ortelius and others remarked on the jigsaw fit of the continents centuries before him. Wegener's originality, first put to geologists in a 1912 lecture, lay in combining that fit with fossil, rock and climate evidence.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-wegener-the-first-to-notice-the-continents-fit-together.html)

Round 9 · No. 85

### [Was umami discovered in a seaweed broth?](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-umami-discovered-in-a-seaweed-broth.html)

TRUE

**True.** In 1908 the Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda isolated glutamate from kombu seaweed broth, coined the word umami and developed MSG as a seasoning. Umami is now widely accepted as the fifth basic taste.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-umami-discovered-in-a-seaweed-broth.html)

Round 9 · No. 86

### [Did Mendeleev invent the periodic table alone?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-mendeleev-invent-the-periodic-table-alone.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Dmitri Mendeleev published his periodic table in 1869, but he did not conceive it alone. John Newlands had proposed a related law of octaves in 1865, and Julius Lothar Meyer worked out a similar arrangement independently at about the same time.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-mendeleev-invent-the-periodic-table-alone.html)

Round 9 · No. 87

### [Were Mendel's pea results too good to be true?](https://conyso.com/publishing/were-mendels-pea-results-too-good-to-be-true.html)

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** In 1936 Fisher began a statistical debate over whether Gregor Mendel's reported ratios fit too closely to be chance. The record calls the question unresolved, not a proven charge of fabrication.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/were-mendels-pea-results-too-good-to-be-true.html)

Round 9 · No. 88

### [Did Gauss guess the prime number theorem as a teenager?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-gauss-guess-the-prime-number-theorem-as-a-teenager.html)

TRUE

**True.** The record reports that Gauss, as a teenager in the 1790s, conjectured the prime number theorem from tables of primes. It was proved only in 1896, about a century later.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-gauss-guess-the-prime-number-theorem-as-a-teenager.html)

Round 9 · No. 89

### [Did Hooke publish his law as an anagram?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-hooke-publish-his-law-as-an-anagram.html)

TRUE

**True.** Robert Hooke published his law of springs in 1676 as the anagram "ceiiinosssttuu." In 1678 he revealed the answer: "ut tensio, sic vis," as the extension, so the force.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-hooke-publish-his-law-as-an-anagram.html)

Round 9 · No. 90

### [Was the 1919 eclipse a clean proof of Einstein?](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-the-1919-eclipse-a-clean-proof-of-einstein.html)

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** The 1919 eclipse measurements matched Einstein's prediction, and modern reanalyses largely uphold the result. But the proof was not clean: blurred plates from one telescope were discarded, and historians have debated whether that was justified.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/was-the-1919-eclipse-a-clean-proof-of-einstein.html)

## Answer key

1. Was Photo 51 taken by Raymond Gosling? **TRUE**
2. Did Watson and Crick steal Rosalind Franklin's data? **DISPUTED**
3. Did Philippa Foot invent the trolley problem? **TRUE**
4. Was Wegener the first to notice the continents fit together? **FOLKLORE**
5. Was umami discovered in a seaweed broth? **TRUE**
6. Did Mendeleev invent the periodic table alone? **FOLKLORE**
7. Were Mendel's pea results too good to be true? **DISPUTED**
8. Did Gauss guess the prime number theorem as a teenager? **TRUE**
9. Did Hooke publish his law as an anagram? **TRUE**
10. Was the 1919 eclipse a clean proof of Einstein? **DISPUTED**

# Round 10: Money, power and policy

> Round 10 of True or Folklore?, money, power and policy: Bounties, bombs and bad incentives. Play free online, then see each verdict and its source.

True or Folklore? · Round 10 of 10

# Round 10: Money, power and policy

Bounties, bombs and bad incentives. Make your call on each story, then tap to see the verdict.

Your score

–

Make a call to start

Playing at a table?

Read each question aloud. Everyone writes TRUE, FOLKLORE or DISPUTED before anyone taps. One point for each right call; DISPUTED only scores if the call was DISPUTED. The book has a two-team scoresheet for this.

Round 10 · No. 91

### [Did a cobra bounty in Delhi breed more cobras?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-a-cobra-bounty-in-delhi-breed-more-cobras.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** No record shows that anyone in Delhi bred cobras for a bounty. The idea the story named rests on firmer evidence, which is the next story in this round.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-a-cobra-bounty-in-delhi-breed-more-cobras.html)

Round 10 · No. 92

### [Did a French bounty on rat tails in Hanoi backfire?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-a-french-bounty-on-rat-tails-in-hanoi-backfire.html)

TRUE

**True.** In 1902 the French colonial administration in Hanoi paid a bounty for each rat killed, with a severed tail as proof. Rat-catchers began cutting the tails off live rats and letting them go to breed. The case is documented in a 2003 paper by M. G. Vann in *French Colonial History*.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-a-french-bounty-on-rat-tails-in-hanoi-backfire.html)

Round 10 · No. 93

### [Did more efficient steam engines make Britain burn more coal?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-more-efficient-steam-engines-make-britain-burn-more-coal.html)

TRUE

**True.** In *The Coal Question* (1865), the economist William Stanley Jevons observed that England's coal use soared after more efficient steam engines expanded coal's industrial uses.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-more-efficient-steam-engines-make-britain-burn-more-coal.html)

Round 10 · No. 95

### [Did broken-windows policing cause New York's 1990s crime drop?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-broken-windows-policing-cause-new-yorks-1990s-crime-drop.html)

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** The claim that broken-windows policing caused New York's crime decline is disputed and confounded. Crime fell across most American cities in the 1990s, including cities that never adopted the approach, and a 2006 analysis by Harcourt and Ludwig found little causal support for the crime-reduction claim.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-broken-windows-policing-cause-new-yorks-1990s-crime-drop.html)

Round 10 · No. 98

### [Did the Sydney Opera House open a decade late and vastly over budget?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-the-sydney-opera-house-open-a-decade-late-and-vastly-over-budget.html)

TRUE

**True.** The Sydney Opera House was estimated to open in 1963 at a cost of a few million pounds. A scaled-down version opened in 1973 at A$102 million. The exact figures vary by source.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-the-sydney-opera-house-open-a-decade-late-and-vastly-over-budget.html)

Round 10 · No. 99

### [Did Hardin later admit the tragedy of the commons was missing a word?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-hardin-later-admit-the-tragedy-of-the-commons-was-missing-a-word.html)

TRUE

**True.** Garrett Hardin later conceded that his error had been to omit one word: "unmanaged." His tragedy describes an unmanaged, open-access resource, not every shared one.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-hardin-later-admit-the-tragedy-of-the-commons-was-missing-a-word.html)

Round 10 · No. 100

### [Did Garrett Hardin invent the overgrazed-pasture parable?](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-garrett-hardin-invent-the-overgrazed-pasture-parable.html)

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** The overgrazed-pasture parable came from William Forster Lloyd in 1833. Garrett Hardin named the idea and popularized it in 1968, 135 years later.

[The answer and its source →](https://conyso.com/publishing/did-garrett-hardin-invent-the-overgrazed-pasture-parable.html)

# True or Folklore?

100 Famous Stories You've Been Told Wrong: The Myth-Busting Quiz for Curious Minds

Edited by [Krishna Chagti](https://conyso.com/publishing/editor.html) · Conyso Publishing · Paperback and Kindle planned

[Play round 1 free](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-01.html) See the ten rounds

## Did Newton get hit by an apple? Did Archimedes really shout "Eureka!" in the bath? Did Galileo drop balls from the Leaning Tower?

Everyone has heard these stories. Fewer people know which ones actually happened.

**True or Folklore?** puts 100 famous stories from science, history, money and the mind to the test. Each one starts as a question on its own page, with a cartoon and three boxes to tick: **TRUE**, **FOLKLORE** or **DISPUTED**. Then turn the page for the verdict, the real story, why the myth spread, and the earliest source that settles it.

### The gift

- A page at the front to write who it's for
- Score titles from "Easily Fooled" to "Myth Buster" to argue over
- A "Tell someone" fact at the end of every answer, for the next dinner conversation

### What they'll keep using

- **100 stories in 10 ready-made quiz rounds** for game nights, with a two-team scoresheet
- **Two minutes per story**, so it works for a commute or a coffee break
- **Every verdict checked against the record**, with the source named on the page. Eighteen stories are still genuinely disputed, and the book says so
- A page of ideas for using it in class

48 FOLKLORE

34 TRUE

18 DISPUTED

## What does the book have that this site doesn't?

- **The full answers.** The site gives each verdict and the fact worth repeating. The book adds the real story, why the myth spread and the earliest source, about two minutes a story.
- **All 100 stories.** 92 are online so far; the rest go up once their verdicts are final.
- **A cartoon for every question**, a two-team scoresheet, score titles and a page of classroom ideas.
- **Paper.** No screen at the table, nothing to log into.

Not on sale yet, so there is no store link or price here. The day it is, this page and [the Law Tome's books page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/books/) will link to it.

Every round is playable here. Each story page gives the verdict, the fact worth repeating and the source; the full answers and the cartoons are in the book.

## Where do the stories come from?

The Law Tome series is built from [the Law Tome](https://conyso.com/lawtome/), a free, sourced directory of more than a thousand named laws, effects and principles. Each answer links back to the law it comes from. The text is drafted with AI from sourced records and checked against those sources. The illustrations are made with AI. Corrections found after print are listed on the [errata page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/), and the Law Tome's [books page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/books/) lists every title built from it.

## Questions about the book

Who is True or Folklore? for?

Anyone who likes being the person who knows the real version: quiz hosts, family tables, classrooms and curious readers. It is written as a gift, with a page at the front to write who it is for.

How long does each story take?

About two minutes: the question on one page, the answer on the next. That makes it work for a commute, a coffee break or a round at a party.

How many of the stories are true?

34 of the 100. 48 are folklore, and 18 are still genuinely disputed, which the book says rather than pretending to settle.

Where do the verdicts come from?

From [the Law Tome](https://conyso.com/lawtome/)'s sourced records, checked again against a primary source, or the best available, for the book. The source is named on the page.

What age is it for?

It is written for adults and teens. A few stories deal with a murder, war and psychology experiments that harmed people, so read a round before using it with younger students.

What formats will it come in?

Paperback and Kindle are planned. There is no store link yet because it is not on sale yet.

# Was Benford's law first spotted in worn logarithm tables?

> Was Benford's law first spotted in worn logarithm tables? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/was-benfords-law-first-spotted-in-worn-logarithm-tables.html

Story No. 38 · [Round 4: Charts and numbers](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-04.html)

# Was Benford's law first spotted in worn logarithm tables?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** The astronomer Simon Newcomb first noticed the leading-digit law in 1881, from the observation that the early pages of logarithm tables, those for numbers starting with 1, were the most worn. Frank Benford rediscovered it in 1938.

Tell someone: Simon Newcomb first spotted Benford's law in 1881, noticing that the early pages of logarithm tables, for numbers starting with 1, were the most worn.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version credits Frank Benford with the discovery, as the name suggests.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Stony Brook / AMS Feature Column page on Newcomb](https://math.stonybrook.edu/~tony/whatsnew/mar09/newcomb.html)
- ["Benford's law," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benford%27s_law)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Newcomb, "Note on the Frequency of Use of the Different Digits in Natural Numbers," *American Journal of Mathematics* 4 (1881). Benford, "The Law of Anomalous Numbers," *Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society* 78(4) (1938). "Benford's law," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/benfords-law/).

# Was Hubble the first to find Hubble's law?

> Was Hubble the first to find Hubble's law? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/was-hubble-the-first-to-find-hubbles-law.html

Story No. 45 · [Round 5: Names that mislead](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-05.html)

# Was Hubble the first to find Hubble's law?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Georges Lemaître derived the relation between a galaxy's distance and its speed of recession, and estimated its constant, in 1927. Edwin Hubble's paper came two years later, in 1929. In 2018 the International Astronomical Union recommended renaming the law the Hubble–Lemaître law.

Tell someone: Georges Lemaître derived Hubble's law in 1927, two years before Hubble's paper, and since 2018 the IAU recommends calling it the Hubble–Lemaître law.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version credits Hubble alone with discovering, in 1929, that the universe is expanding.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Luminet, "The Rise of Big Bang Models (4): Lemaître"](https://blogs.futura-sciences.com/e-luminet/2015/06/21/the-rise-of-big-bang-models-4-lemaitre/)
- [Astronomy, "IAU vote recommends changing the name of Hubble's law"](https://www.astronomy.com/science/iau-vote-recommends-changing-the-name-of-hubbles-law/)
- [Kragh, "Hubble Law or Hubble-Lemaître Law? The IAU Resolution," arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.02557)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Lemaître, "Un univers homogène de masse constante et de rayon croissant…," *Annales de la Société Scientifique de Bruxelles* (1927). IAU, "IAU members vote to recommend renaming the Hubble law as the Hubble–Lemaître law" (2018). "Hubble's law," Wikipedia. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/hubbles-law/).

# Was "moving the goalposts" used in Parliament a century ago?

> Was "moving the goalposts" used in Parliament a century ago? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/was-moving-the-goalposts-used-in-parliament-a-century-ago.html

Story No. 68 · [Round 7: Words and phrases](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-07.html)

# Was "moving the goalposts" used in Parliament a century ago?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** The earliest documented figurative use of the phrase is in a House of Commons debate on 2 May 1924. The idiom is British, and it was in political speech some sixty years before it came into widespread use in the 1980s.

Tell someone: In the House of Commons on 2 May 1924, the Labour MP George Hardie said the Liberals "wanted to shift the goal posts."

## What's the version people tell?

The popular assumption dates the phrase to the 1980s and files it with that decade's business jargon.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [wordhistories.net](https://wordhistories.net/2019/08/09/move-goalposts-british/)
- [phrases.org.uk](https://www.phrases.org.uk/meanings/251400.html)
- ["David Leggio," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Leggio)
- ["Moving the goalposts," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moving_the_goalposts)
- [historic Hansard index, May 1924](https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/sittings/1924/may)

> Was Photo 51 taken by Raymond Gosling? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Story No. 81 · [Round 9: Discovery stories](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-09.html)

# Was Photo 51 taken by Raymond Gosling?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** Raymond Gosling, a doctoral student, took Photo 51 at King's College London in May 1952, while working under Rosalind Franklin's supervision. The credit belongs to both of them.

Tell someone: Photo 51 was taken by Raymond Gosling, a doctoral student, in May 1952, using Rosalind Franklin's fibers and working under her supervision.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version gives the photograph to Franklin alone. She is the person the image is most closely associated with, and the short telling of the DNA story has no room for her student.

## What's the source?

Cited in the book: "The story behind Photograph 51," King's College London. "Photo 51," Wikipedia. Cobb and Comfort, *Nature* (2023). The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/photo-51/).

# Was Schrödinger's cat meant to make a quantum idea look absurd?

> Was Schrödinger's cat meant to make a quantum idea look absurd? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/was-schrodingers-cat-meant-to-make-a-quantum-idea-look-absurd.html

Story No. 54 · [Round 6: Physics in the kitchen and the sky](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-06.html)

# Was Schrödinger's cat meant to make a quantum idea look absurd?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** Erwin Schrödinger devised the cat in 1935 as an objection to the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics. His aim was to show the absurdity of extending quantum superposition to a large object, not to claim that a cat can be alive and dead at once.

Tell someone: Schrödinger's cat was a critique: he devised it in 1935 to show that extending quantum superposition to a large object is absurd.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version turns the argument around: Schrödinger proposed that a cat in a sealed box really is both alive and dead until someone looks.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- ["Schrödinger's cat," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schr%C3%B6dinger%27s_cat)
- ["The Role of Decoherence in Quantum Mechanics," *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qm-decoherence/)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Schrödinger, "Die gegenwärtige Situation in der Quantenmechanik," *Naturwissenschaften* 23 (1935). "Schrödinger's cat," Wikipedia. "Schrödinger's cat," *Encyclopaedia Britannica*. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/schrodingers-cat/).

# Was the 1919 eclipse a clean proof of Einstein?

> Was the 1919 eclipse a clean proof of Einstein? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/was-the-1919-eclipse-a-clean-proof-of-einstein.html

Story No. 90 · [Round 9: Discovery stories](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-09.html)

# Was the 1919 eclipse a clean proof of Einstein?

Just show me the answer

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** The 1919 eclipse measurements matched Einstein's prediction, and modern reanalyses largely uphold the result. But the proof was not clean: blurred plates from one telescope were discarded, and historians have debated whether that was justified.

Tell someone: The 1919 eclipse results matched Einstein and have largely survived reanalysis, though blurred plates from one Sobral telescope were set aside, a choice historians debated.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is a single triumphant photograph. Eddington's plates proved relativity beyond doubt.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Longair, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A (2015)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4360090/)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

# Was the acronym "MAD" a critic's jibe?

> Was the acronym "MAD" a critic's jibe? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/was-the-acronym-mad-a-critics-jibe.html

Story No. 67 · [Round 7: Words and phrases](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-07.html)

# Was the acronym "MAD" a critic's jibe?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** The acronym MAD is attributed to a critic, Donald Brennan of the Hudson Institute, who used it derisively to argue that the nuclear posture it named was irrational. Robert McNamara, under whom the doctrine took shape, promoted "assured destruction," not MAD.

Tell someone: McNamara called it "assured destruction"; the acronym MAD is attributed to Donald Brennan, a critic who used it derisively, so the initials spell the charge.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version holds that MAD was the Pentagon's own acronym, a name the planners gave their strategy.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [McNamara speech, Atomic Archive](https://www.atomicarchive.com/Docs/Deterrence/Deterrence.shtml)
- ["Mutual assured destruction," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutual_assured_destruction)
- ["The Making of MAD," Air & Space Forces Magazine](https://www.airandspaceforces.com/article/the-making-of-mad/)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: "Mutual assured destruction," *Encyclopaedia Britannica*. McNamara, "Mutual Deterrence" speech, San Francisco, 18 September 1967 (Atomic Archive text). The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/mutual-assured-destruction/).

# Was the Doppler effect tested with trumpeters on a train?

> Was the Doppler effect tested with trumpeters on a train? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Story No. 60 · [Round 6: Physics in the kitchen and the sky](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-06.html)

# Was the Doppler effect tested with trumpeters on a train?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** C. H. D. Buys Ballot tested the Doppler effect for sound in 1845, using trumpeters on a moving train. Christian Doppler had predicted the effect three years earlier, in an 1842 paper in Prague.

Tell someone: The trumpeters were real: in 1845 Buys Ballot tested the Doppler effect for sound on a moving train, three years after Doppler predicted it.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular assumption is that the trumpeters belong in a textbook, not a railway timetable: the scene sounds like an illustration invented to explain a passing siren, not an experiment anyone ran.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Nolte, *Physics Today*](https://physicstoday.aip.org/features/the-fall-and-rise-of-the-doppler-effect)

# Was the forgetting curve based on just one person?

> Was the forgetting curve based on just one person? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/was-the-forgetting-curve-based-on-just-one-person.html

Story No. 29 · [Round 3: Famous experiments, retold](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-03.html)

# Was the forgetting curve based on just one person?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** The forgetting curve rests on one subject: Hermann Ebbinghaus, who tested himself. Its best-known modern replication, in 2015, also used essentially one subject.

Tell someone: The forgetting curve was measured on one man, Ebbinghaus, learning nonsense syllables, and its 2015 replication again used essentially one subject.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version treats the curve as a general law of memory, measured across many people and describing how everyone forgets.

## What's the source?

# Was the Overton window named only after Overton's death?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** Joseph P. Overton developed the idea in the mid-1990s, but it was his colleague Joseph Lehman who named and elaborated it, after Overton died in a 2003 ultralight-aircraft crash.

Tell someone: Joseph Overton developed the idea, but his colleague Joseph Lehman named it the Overton window only after Overton died in 2003.

The popular version assumes that Overton coined "the Overton window" himself.

# Was the Peter Principle written as satire?

> Was the Peter Principle written as satire? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/was-the-peter-principle-written-as-satire.html

Story No. 72 · [Round 8: Jokes that became laws](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-08.html)

# Was the Peter Principle written as satire?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** The Peter Principle was pitched as satire. The educator Laurence J. Peter and the playwright Raymond Hull set it out in their 1969 book: "In a hierarchy, every employee tends to rise to his level of incompetence." It landed as serious management theory.

Tell someone: The Peter Principle was pitched as satire, written in 1969 by an educator and a playwright under the subtitle *Why Things Always Go Wrong*.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version treats the principle as a finding of management research, a measured law of how organizations promote people.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- ["Peter principle," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_principle)
- [AbeBooks listing, ISBN 0285502557](https://www.abebooks.com/9780285502550/Peter-Principle-Why-Things-Always-0285502557/plp)
- ["Putt's Law and the Successful Technocrat," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Putt%27s_Law_and_the_Successful_Technocrat)

Story No. 73 · [Round 8: Jokes that became laws](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-08.html)

# Was there a real committee that argued over a bike shed?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** No real meeting lies behind the story. The reactor, the bicycle shed and the refreshment budget are C. Northcote Parkinson's invented example, from his 1957 book *Parkinson's Law, or The Pursuit of Progress*.

Tell someone: The committee that approved a reactor in minutes and argued over a bike shed never met; C. Northcote Parkinson invented it in 1957.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version reports it as something that happened: a committee approved a nuclear reactor in minutes and then argued for far longer about a bike shed.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- ["Law of triviality," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_triviality)
- [Kamp email, bikeshed.org](https://bikeshed.org/)

# Was umami discovered in a seaweed broth?

> Was umami discovered in a seaweed broth? Make your call, then see the verdict, the one fact worth repeating and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/was-umami-discovered-in-a-seaweed-broth.html

Story No. 85 · [Round 9: Discovery stories](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-09.html)

# Was umami discovered in a seaweed broth?

Just show me the answer

TRUE

**True.** In 1908 the Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda isolated glutamate from kombu seaweed broth, coined the word umami and developed MSG as a seasoning. Umami is now widely accepted as the fifth basic taste.

Tell someone: Umami was found in kombu seaweed broth: Kikunae Ikeda isolated glutamate there in 1908 and named the taste before developing MSG.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is skeptical. On this telling, umami is a marketing invention: a word made up to sell a seasoning, not a taste in its own right.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Ikeda, "New Seasonings," Chemical Senses](https://academic.oup.com/chemse/article/27/9/847/273933)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

# Was Wegener the first to notice the continents fit together?

> Was Wegener the first to notice the continents fit together? Guess first, then see the verdict and the source that settles it.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/was-wegener-the-first-to-notice-the-continents-fit-together.html

Story No. 84 · [Round 9: Discovery stories](https://conyso.com/publishing/round-09.html)

# Was Wegener the first to notice the continents fit together?

Just show me the answer

FOLKLORE

**Folklore.** Alfred Wegener was not the first. Ortelius and others remarked on the jigsaw fit of the continents centuries before him. Wegener's originality, first put to geologists in a 1912 lecture, lay in combining that fit with fossil, rock and climate evidence.

Tell someone: Ortelius and others remarked on the jigsaw fit of the continents centuries before Wegener; his real feat was adding fossils, rocks and ancient climates.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version has Wegener looking at a map, seeing South America nest into Africa and spotting the jigsaw.

## What's the source?

Checked on 12 November 2026 against

- ["Abraham Ortelius," Wikipedia, quoting Kious and Tilling (USGS)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Ortelius)

The text was drafted with AI from the Law Tome record. A person then opened these sources and checked the verdict against them. Found a mistake? It goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Cited in the book: Ortelius, *Thesaurus Geographicus* (1596). Romm, "A New Forerunner for Continental Drift," *Nature* 367 (1994). Wegener, "Die Entstehung der Kontinente," *Geologische Rundschau* 3 (1912). "Alfred Wegener," *Encyclopaedia Britannica*. "Wegener's Puzzling Continental Drift Evidence," USGS. The full list is on [the Law Tome's entry](https://conyso.com/lawtome/laws/continental-drift/).

# Were Mendel's pea results too good to be true?

# Were Mendel's pea results too good to be true?

Just show me the answer

DISPUTED

**Disputed.** In 1936 Fisher began a statistical debate over whether Gregor Mendel's reported ratios fit too closely to be chance. The record calls the question unresolved, not a proven charge of fabrication.

Tell someone: Since Fisher in 1936, statisticians have argued over whether Mendel's pea ratios fit too well, and no one has settled it either way.

## What's the version people tell?

The popular version is short: Mendel fudged his data.
